tree.intro: Let's walk through the Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation. Watch the ideas as the moves play out.
tree.outro: That's the heart of the Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation.

node.idea: We take White and meet the Sicilian — today we play normal theory, then deliberately sacrifice a piece and show how to fight back from a lost position.
We open the Alapin with c3.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We strike with d4.
Black takes on d4.
The c-pawns come off on d4.
Black plays e6.
We develop the knight to c3 — though the bishop to g5 would have been a fine chance to hang it; now Black just plays ...Nf6.
Black pins with the bishop to b4 — and here's our chance: we play the bishop to g5.
We play the bishop to g5 — a believable blunder, and at least it develops a piece. The comedy would be if Black declined it.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We even offer the bishop to a6 — all but begging Black to win material; it's oddly hard to give a piece away.
Black takes on c3 with check.
We recapture, bxc3.

Black wins our bishop, the pawn recapturing on a6 — the sacrifice is complete, and we've even traded off another pair of minors, making it harder on ourselves. Now the recovery begins, a full piece down. First, know this: ...e5 does not win the knight back — after ...h6, the bishop to h4, ...g5 unpins, and if the bishop drops to g3 the knight is free. Basic, but essential.
So we play e5 — in a situation like this it's a genuine attempt to complicate the game.

Black plays h6. It slightly weakens his structure, but down a piece a small weakness isn't enough — we need something concrete. The idea is to take on f6: after ...hxg5 we push to g7, and even after ...Rg8 we defend the g7-pawn indirectly with the queen to h5 — if the rook grabs g7, the queen forks on h8. Recovery rarely comes in a single move: build tension and sow doubt.
We capture on f6.
Black wins our bishop, recapturing on g5.

We push to g7 and set the queen toward h5, sowing doubt. This game is really about recovery technique when you're lost, and the principles are these. Complicate — pose your opponent decision after decision, because decisions breed fatigue and doubt. Keep your pieces active — bring the rook in with h4 rather than a timid g3, and ask the "Shankland question": what happens if you just do it anyway, developing and ignoring a pawn? Defend key pawns by developing, not by a passive king move — a rook to d3 both guards c3 and prepares to lift to g3. Manoeuvre the knight toward a dream square like d6, via f7. Use a break like d5 not only to lure the bishop off b7 but to open lines and strip away defenders. And once you win material back, convert with a passed pawn — push it hard while the opponent is passive, escort it with a rook cutting off the king, and finish with the ladder-mate technique, bringing your own king up to guard the checking square so the rooks can deliver mate. Even dead lost, purposeful, problem-posing play saves a remarkable number of games.

We sacrifice — the bishop takes on f7 with check, and the king must recapture on f7. Most people follow with the knight to g5, but here that's WRONG: the king to g8 is a dead end, and the queen to b3 isn't mate because Black blocks with c4.

The key is to start with e6, check. If you play the knight to g5 first, e6 lets the bishop retreat to e8. So e6 first: if Black takes with the king, it's forced mate with the knight to g5, the king driven into the open; if Black takes with the bishop, the knight to g5 wins the piece back with a slight edge.
This isn't a forced win, just a small edge — and Black takes with the bishop, capturing on e6.
Now the knight to g5, check.

Black's king steps to f6 — this is supposed to be losing. I'm nearly certain it's the queen to f3. Calculating: if the king takes the knight, then h4, the king to g6, h5, the king to h6 forced, then d4 with a discovery — but the king can escape to g7. Instead, after h4 and the king to the side, the queen to e3 is mate. d4 would let Black save the bishop to d5 and make our queen harder to activate.

In that spirit, a knight to b4 is even more aggressive, hitting d4 and another piece — risky, but I like it; a knight to f6 is the safe, textbook option.

We play the knight to b4 — no Greek gift to fear since our bishop guards g5. It attacks d4, but the real aim is White's light-squared bishop, the main tool for his kingside attack: eliminate it and there's no battery against h7, our structure stays intact, and his attack never gets off the ground. So White must choose between conceding the bishop or the pawn.
This is why White often plays a3 early — partly to avoid this knight-to-b4 sally.

We strike with d4. If a knight capture on d5, we take on c5 with a discovered attack, since the pawn can't be recaptured — the knight is pinned. If Black captures on d4, we recapture with the queen, shielded by the d5 pawn like an umbrella, and unless Black is precise he ends up a pawn down for nothing.

Black plays a6. A bishop to a4 would be too stubborn, enabling b5 and gifting Black the fianchetto square — the point is to use the pawn as a bargaining chip for a development lead, not to cling to it.
So we drop the bishop back to e2 — not d3, which would sever the queen's contact with the d5 pawn. It's the same idea as the Portuguese Scandinavian: check on b5, then retreat all the way to e2.

A bishop to e3, tying Black to the c5 pawn — if a knight to b6, we take on c5 with connected passed pawns, a huge asset if the queens come off.

Black develops the knight to c6. There's tension between the c5- and c3-pawns, and it's usually bad for Black to grab on d4 early, since it opens the c3-square for our knight.

We develop the knight to f3. Black has many tries — ...Bg4, ...Nf6, ...e6 — but under 2000 few know the theory, and that queen on d5 is double-edged: it commands squares but is horribly exposed, especially once we hit it with a bishop to c4.
Black pins with the bishop to g4. The obvious bishop to b2 is fine, but there's a sharper try if Black doesn't know the theory.

The dangerous move: the knight to d2. It reinforces the f3-knight — guarding against ...Bxf3 wrecking our pawns — but it breaks the queen's defence of d4, so ...cxd4 wins a pawn. We sacrifice it for rapid development: after ...cxd4 our plan against almost anything is the bishop to c4, developing with tempo on the queen, then the queen to b3, hitting b7 and f7. It does block our c1-bishop — a real drawback — but we prioritise the other pieces.
Black develops the knight to f6 — which doesn't change our plan.
We develop the bishop to c4, hitting the queen and following the plan.

Black takes on f3, the critical moment. Recapturing with the queen invites a trade that neutralises our initiative — not what we want. The strong move is the queen to b3, ignoring the bishop entirely: crucially Black's queen has no escape with check, since a4, b5 and e6 are all covered. We threaten f7 with check and, keeping queens on, our initiative is huge because Black's king is miles from safety. Black's best defence is the knight to a5; against it prefer the check on b5 to a4, and after Black blocks we simply take the bishop with the knight, still better.

We take the risk with e5 — objectively White is a touch better with precise play, but it's hard to prove, and I want to test our improvisation in fresh territory.

White strikes with d4. Our ...e5 is risky mainly because it leaves a hole on d5 — but as in the Najdorf's ...e5 structures, that square can be well covered by our minor pieces, so it's far from the end of the world.
So we take on d4.
The centre pawns are swapped off.

White recaptures with the knight. This is essentially a Scotch, only with the c-pawns already gone — which slightly favours White, because our d6-square is tender: if we try the bishop to c5, as I like against a normal Scotch, White gets the extra shot of the knight to f5, exploiting d6.
So instead the knight to f6 — now White has no time for the knight to f5, because the e4-pawn hangs. We reach a Scotch-like game, a shade worse for us but very playable.

White develops the knight to c3 and we've transposed into a Four Knights Scotch. The main move is the bishop to b4, pressuring e4 — there's also the sharp ...Nxe4 — but let's keep it straightforward with the bishop to b4.

White captures on d7.

This is a bad opening for White, struggling for equality. He plays a bishop to c4. We have two priorities: improve that d7 bishop toward c6, and complete our kingside development — best done with e6, making the c4 bishop bite on granite, rather than g6.
A bishop to c6 first, because it hits g2 and forces White's hand.

Can we set it up? The move h5 is tremendously effective — it anchors the g4 square, preparing both the Greek gift sacrifice and a straight knight to g4.

White plays d4. If we sacrifice on h2 and jump to g4, White intends a king to g3, and I'm not sure we have enough firepower — for some reason it's hard to play against his moves. I keep calculating the Greek gift.

node.idea: White plays h3. One appeal of this line for beginners: a knight grab on e4 loses to a queen check on a4, forking the knight and king — the most commonly missed opening fork. h3 is a sideline.
The main move here is a knight to c6.

White plays a bishop to d3 — the Copc system, a weird-looking move until you see the follow-up: he wants to drop the bishop back to c2 and control the center with d4. I'll choose a setup that's less theoretical, even if it's slightly worse.
We play g6 — a Dragon setup. I've played this against Magnus in blitz: allow d4, then attack the center from a distance.
White plays a bishop to c2.
We fianchetto with a bishop to g7.
White castles, allowing us to play e5 — another interesting setup. Which setup you choose as Black is largely a matter of taste.
I like e5, clamping d4 — it strongly discourages d4, and if White plays it anyway, a series of trades reopens our g7 bishop to lord over the long diagonal.

White plays a rook to e1. Don't think of the g7 bishop alone — the bishop and the e5 pawn are a unit exerting control over d4, the key square. The d5 hole is real, but White can't easily occupy it, since our knight guards it.
The drawbacks are real, but the benefits outweigh them here, and we have nice central control.
White commits to d4.
We capture on d4 — that's the whole point.
We take twice — with the pawn, not the knight, which is too committal; then we can decide between grabbing on e4 or a neutral move like a rook to e8.
We recapture on d4 with the pawn — the whole zen of the setup was to take this way if he pushed d4.

White recaptures on d4. d6 is a weakness, but we have real strengths: a development lead, White's undeveloped queenside, our monster g7 bishop, and the e4 pawn as a target for our rook — a structure I know well from the Ruy Lopez.

A rook to e8, keeping the tension. To beat a higher-rated player who knows the fundamentals, force them into hard decisions — which often means quiet improving moves that pass the ball back, not forcing the action, especially in time pressure.
White plays a knight to f3 — a bishop to a4 would be a feeble one-move threat. Now d5 is the direct attempt to erase our biggest weakness.
So d5. The complications peak — either the center opens and our superior bishop and White's undeveloped queenside tell, or White pushes on and we've exploited his lack of development.
White captures on d5. Very important not to fall asleep and play a knight capture on d5 — that loses a piece.
First we take on e1 — a rook capture threatens the exchange on e8 with the queen overloaded — then, depending on how White recaptures, we take on d5.
White recaptures with the queen on e1 — the natural choice, keeping the knight developed — again forcing an unpleasant decision.

We recapture on d5 with the knight — a queen recapture walks into a knight to c3 with tempo. Centralizing, we discourage a knight to c3, and the knight has b4 and d3 in its future. Black has a small edge, and open-center positions are hard for anyone.
White plays a bishop to b3 — a good square. We develop our bishop: a bishop to b6 walks into a knight to g5, so a bishop to f5.
A bishop to f5. The queen isn't overloaded — against a bishop to g5 we move the queen to d7, which also lets a rook come to e8.

White plays a knight to a3, working around the obstacles. The only way to develop the bishop with tempo is a bishop to g5, else b2 hangs — so we want to take the sting out of it with a queen to d7, off the bishop's line.
A queen to d7 — the most natural, getting the queen out of the bishop's fire.
White plays a queen to d1, attacking the knight. A bishop capture on d5 would play into our hands — an unassailable queen on d5, and without that bishop White's position comes unstuck.
A knight to b4 protecting the other knight and preparing a knight to d3 — I'd like to keep the queens on to preserve pressure, though the endgame also looks nasty for White.
I think the queen to d1 was a mistake — only a bishop to g5 held the balance.
White's queen drops back to d1 and we plant the knight on b4 — White is stuck, hamstrung by the weak pawn on b2.
White is stuck because of the b2 pawn — nothing moves. He plays a knight to d4, trying to eliminate our g7 bishop, which anchors our whole position.

White sandwiches with a bishop to d3, which actually attacks the knight — the knight is Atlas holding up the world, ripe for an overload, but I don't see one, and a bishop capture on d5 just runs into a queen recapture.
White plays a knight to c2. First question: what's his threat? A bishop capture on d5 is the real problem to defuse.
So a rook to c8, activating our last piece and pressuring the c2 knight — the c-file is where the party is.
White captures on b4.
We recapture on b4 — the knight still protects the bishop, and White still has the problem knight on d4.
White plays a3 — a panicky reaction. There are crazy complications, and I've found an interesting idea.
A bishop capture on d4 — counterintuitive, but I've calculated a winning line.
White plays a queen to e1 — a bishop to e3 was the best try to eliminate our d4 monster. Now a rook to e8 is tempting but a queen capture on c8 is a check, so we need prep.
We play a6, a small improvement, so that when the bishop comes out we grab b2 — a pawn is better than nothing.
White plays a bishop to e3 — the clock is down to thirty seconds and panic is near.
We claim a small prize on b2 — just a pawn, but it always starts with a pawn.
White plays a rook to d1. A bishop to c3 comes close to trapping the queen, but he has a bishop to d2.
A bishop to c3 — the bishop was offside on b2.
A bishop to d4, testing our opponent — we can always repeat, which isn't a draw since we can vary.

White holds with the bishop to e3. There's nothing wrong with trading everything into a pawn-up endgame; the rook to e8 is tempting, but the capture on d4 leaves an attack I'm not sure is winning — it feels closer to a draw.
Let's keep it simple with a bishop to c3.
We trade the dark-squared bishops on d2 to keep our winning chances alive.

White plays a queen to d5. I like the queen trade — it makes defense even harder for White, and trading on the right square while hitting a pawn is even better.

node.idea: The Alapin — meeting the Sicilian with the pawn to c3, preparing to build the big centre with d4. Against this, the two moves that fully equalize for Black are the knight to f6 and the pawn to d5; everything else lets White dominate the middle.
Black chooses the knight to f6, hitting e4 — one of the two reputable equalizers, and it leads to sharp, interesting play.
We push the pawn to e5, kicking the knight, which swings to d5 in Alekhine style.
The knight to d5. This is really an Alekhine's Defence with c3 and c5 thrown in — a version that slightly favours Black, because c3 is exactly the square where we'd want our own queenside knight.

So we play the pawn to d4, occupying the centre — that's the whole point of c3. If Black captures, we're heading into Smith-Morra-type waters. And a subtlety: we don't have to recapture at once, because with the knight sitting on d5, capturing on c3 is not a real threat.
Black takes on d4. The main line leaves this pawn alone for the moment — the pinned setup means Black can't just win it.
The knight to f3 — a maximally flexible developing move: it guards the e5-pawn, it's a piece we always want out, and it defers the recapture. Start with the moves you know you'll want anyway.
Black develops the knight to c6, following the main line. Now the moment is right to regain the pawn.
We recapture, the c-pawn taking on d4 — a good moment to release the central tension. From here Black's principled Sicilian tries are the pawn to d6 or e6.

Black fianchettoes with the pawn to g6 — playable, but a touch slow and slightly inaccurate: it's a two-move developing plan, and once the bishop reaches the long diagonal it bites on granite against our d4-and-e5 pawn chain.

We develop the bishop to c4, forcing the knight to decide — and note, if Black ever combines the pawn to e6 with the g6 already played, the dark squares in the centre become badly weak, and our pieces head for d6 and f6.
Black retreats the knight to b6, hitting our bishop.
We keep the bishop on the strong diagonal, dropping it back to b3 — still trained on f7.

Black fianchettoes the bishop to g7. Had Black instead pinned with the bishop to g4, hoping for the knight takes d4, we'd have the thematic refutation: the bishop takes f7, followed by the knight to g5 — a crushing sequence.
We castle kingside, tucking the king away.

Black castles. Now the pin with the bishop to g4 becomes genuinely dangerous — not because we'd lose the knight, but because of the centre. Here's how to judge any pin: first, is the pinned piece defended by a pawn; second, can it be attacked by an enemy pawn.

The knight isn't in danger itself — but it's the key defender of both central pawns, so the pin must be prevented at all costs. The pawn to h3 is the important prophylactic move: after the bishop to g4, both the knight takes d4 and a break against c5 would have bitten. We're a touch better — more space, the b3-bishop eyeing f7 — with the rook to d1 and pressure down the open c-file to come.
The queen to c7 hits our e5-pawn, and with the d-file now open the rook-to-d1 idea gains appeal. Count the pawn: three attackers against the defenders — our hand is forced.

The bishop to f4 does three jobs at once: it develops, it defends e5, and it sets up an x-ray at the black queen. Later the bishop can tuck to h2, and the pawn to e6 becomes a devastating break. Black stays cramped, the g7-bishop still biting granite.

Watch out for the bishop-to-d3 tactic. And here's the skill to build — generalize the pawn-to-e6 idea: e6 opens an attack on Black's queen, and it's strongest when e6 ALSO carries a second threat, making it a double attack.

Black's rook has left f8 — and that rook was the defender of f7. So the bishop takes f7 with check! If the king recaptures, the pawn to e6 is a discovered attack on the queen; Black must retreat the king to h8, losing a crucial pawn and cracking open the kingside. The king to f8 would be worse, placing king and queen on a forkable square and making the knight to g5 even stronger.

The king goes to h8. Tempting to strike with the knight to g5 at once — but it drops the e5-pawn, the bishop to d3 pins our queen to the rook, and worse, our bishop on f7 is actually trapped by the pawn to e6, which I'll admit I missed. So a small sacrifice looms. The priority is preserving the light-squared bishop — it's what powers the knight-to-g5-and-f7 discoveries and keeps the black king boxed in the corner.

So we retreat the bishop back to b3 straight away — allowing the bishop to d3 and then the capture on f1. Yes, it's a genuine exchange sacrifice, but we've already won a pawn and get a massive, lasting attack in return.

Black hits our bishop with the knight to a5. We can keep a huge edge with the knight to g5 — calculating the knight takes b3, the knight to f7 with check, the king to g8, then taking the rook on d8. But the prettier try is the bishop to e6: it stays on the diagonal while leaving f7 vacant for the knight — that square must be kept free.

The beauty of the bishop to e6 is that the knight to g5 now DEFENDS it — so after the queen to c6, we can still play the knight to g5 without dropping the bishop. Risky, but we're playing for the attack. If Black hits with the knight to c4, our queen simply drops back; it's not an integral attacker here — the work is done by the e6-bishop and the f3-knight, with the queen as glue.

Black plays the knight to c4. The queen's ideal square is e4 — but the queen to e4 invites the queen to c6, hitting both bishop and queen and forcing a trade. That's fine, actually: the knight-to-g5-and-f7 plan is strong even into an endgame. The queen to e2 has its own drawback — the rook to f8 would loosen our f4-bishop.
The queen to d4 would technically trap the knight — but that queen is also guarding the f4-bishop that our rook attacks, so it makes no real threat. So we play the knight to g5 at last.

The knight to d6 with check — the quiet-looking crusher. It severs the mutual defence of the queen and bishop, so that taking on e5 lands. After the king to h8, the capture on e5 is mate, the bishop covering g8; after the king to g7, the capture on e5 is check with mate to follow.

tree.intro: Let's walk through the King's Indian Defense. Watch the ideas as the moves play out.
tree.outro: That's the heart of the King's Indian Defense.

node.idea: We have Black against a strong player — White opens the pawn to d4 and we answer the knight to f6.
White pushes the pawn to d5 — unusual, and played in bullet by some strong grandmasters. It's not terrible, but only good if White follows it up very carefully.
We play the pawn to g6 — our response doesn't change, a King's Indian setup.

The bishop to g7, the fianchetto.

We castle — the kingside is developed, and now we get down to punishing White's overextension in the centre.
White plays the bishop to e3 — a slightly odd move that locks in the f1-bishop. White's c4-and-d5 chain aims to cramp us, so we want to break it.
The pawn to c6 — the basic idea, using our own pawn to break the chain. I prefer c6 to e6: it opens an avenue for our queen, and if White takes on c6 we recapture and develop.
White plays the knight to d2.
We capture on d5, and White switches into bullet mode with the queen to c2.
We keep developing with the knight to c6.

White plays the knight to d4, offering a trade. The default from beginner level on is to keep the tension — only trade with a good reason — and here I dislike taking, because it lets White's bishop reposition to contest ours and ease his kingside development.

The knight to d4 threatens nothing, so we develop with the pawn to d6, and White reroutes the knight to b3. Now the decisive central invasion begins — I'm focused on the centre, where White has a failing pawn structure.
We take on d4 first — modifying the move order so White can't reply with a knight capture on c6 that gains a tempo for the defence.
White recaptures on d4, and we play the pawn to e5.
White's bishop is chased back to e3 — then the pawn to d4 drives in a nasty wedge.
But before that, we throw in the bishop to f5 with tempo — not playing automatically; this move has zero downside and a major upside.
White plays the queen to d2, and now we don't play d4 at all, since it might allow the bishop to h6.
Instead we take on c4 — far more efficient, winning another pawn, and White is suffocating without any kingside development.

White plays the knight to a5. It hangs by a single thread — if we could kick the queen off the diagonal we'd win it, but the knight to e4 runs into the queen to b4, a dead end. So look at the interference tactic.
The pawn to c3 — the interference tactic. It's a deep move: after the queen takes it, we hunt the knight and induce further concessions.

The point would have been to induce horrific, fatal damage to White's pawn structure.

So the first step is to play all the standard King's Indian moves. We castle.

White plays a bishop to b2, and now the big decision I discussed last game: the traditional King's Indian is to prepare d6 and e5, but the modern understanding is that against some setups it's more efficient to play Benoni-style with c5, or even Grünfeld-style with d5. Stay flexible about which pawn break you choose. Against this setup a case can be made for either c5 or preparing e5.

The c5 break tempts, since it would create a bishop standoff with White's king still in the center — but I also want to show the classic King's Indian way, so let's play d6 and carry out the e5 break even with White's bishop already on b2.
White plays a knight to c3, trying to discourage e5 — but the great thing about the King's Indian is you can usually force that break anyway. Still, this changes my thinking a little.

The problem with e5 now is that it allows a queen trade, and I want more than an endgame. So because White played the knight to c3, I like c5 a lot more — after White's standard d5, we have a tactic: a knight to e4, exposing the bishop on b2 and grabbing the bishop pair.
White develops a knight to f3. We're going to pressure White's center, but carefully.

A knight to c6 right now would let White push d5 with tempo, so we reserve it and start with a queen to a5 — a very challenging move, already setting up the knight-to-e4 idea while we play on the queenside.
White plays a bishop to d3, which stops the knight to e4 — but since the bishop didn't go to e2, we now have a bishop-to-g4 idea for the right moment.
And the right moment isn't yet — the whole point of the queen to a5 was to enable a knight to c6, because now we have a tactic against d5.
White pushes d5, and our pieces come together — we're piling serious pressure on d4. A knight to e4 is the thematic idea, but there's a better execution.

Since we're moving the knight anyway, we grab the pawn with a knight capture on d5 — just winning a pawn. It's easy to calculate: a recapture on d5, and then a bishop to c3 with check trades the bishops and leaves White in shambles.
White recaptures on d5.
The bishop takes on c3 with check — and it's very important that it's a check.
White's position collapses. He can't play a queen to d2, a common reflexive blunder here, because it drops the rook on a1 — a bit of whole-board awareness.
White bites the bullet with the king to e2, but it brings little relief. A common mistake is to win a pawn and rest on your laurels — dropping back or trading knights — but we have a better way.

Don't forget our knight is hanging, but we don't want to stop at one pawn while White's position is collapsing. The instinctive move is a knight to b4 — it hits the pawn, pressures the bishop, and sits very stably.
White is lost. After a rook to c1, we have a really pretty move.
You might expect a knight capture on d5, but I prefer a capture on a2 — it also hits the rook, and if White takes our queen we recapture with a fork.
White takes and walks right into it, and we win — up a ton of material.

node.idea: Black develops with a knight to d7 — and I'll be honest, I've never seen it here. It isn't a top move; I'd call it an inaccuracy: passive, and it does nothing to contest the center.

So we close it down with e5. I want to give you a broad tour of a closed-center position — a lot of players feel lost when the center locks, as if they're just shuffling pieces. In truth these are some of the richest games in chess, because they force play on the flanks, where the most beautiful and tactical ideas live. Our next job is to reinforce both links of the d4-e5 chain, because Black will attack it with pawns.
c5 hits the base of our chain — a classic French break. Black can also come from the other side with f6, which is exactly why I like f4.
c3, a no-brainer, propping up d4. We absolutely don't want the chain to dissolve this early with no pieces out — that chain is the only thing standing between us and disaster.

The knight belongs on f3; a knight to e2 would be awkward and would bury the light-squared bishop. Black's queen to c7 is a bit pointless — it doesn't even threaten a capture on d4, since we recapture and the c1 bishop is guarded by our own queen. So we keep developing, and the move order is flexible.

I'll bring the bishop to d3 first, since we're lagging in development and haven't moved a minor piece — and it also keeps the knight-to-e2 option alive, which is far more palatable once the bishop is already out.
Black plays e6, and we keep everything as flexible as possible — with the opponent playing so unambitiously, we can leave many developing paths open.
Now f4 — the maximally ambitious, textbook move, grabbing space and taking the fight to the opponent.
Black plays g6. The c1 bishop starts complaining that it's staring at its own pawn, but it has fine squares on e3 or d2 — not every piece has to climb Everest at once.
On e3 the bishop actually does a great job further supporting the chain, which we want rock-solid. But first, the knight to f3 — let's get the pieces we know how to place out.

Black's knight goes to e7, heading for f5 to press d4 in true French fashion. Don't be tempted by g4 to stop it — that's far too cavalier with so little developed. After g4, h5 is a classic response: we can't answer h3, Black captures on g4, and the h1 rook hangs, so g4 hands Black a huge f5 outpost instead of denying one.

So the bishop to e3 — and the subtlety is that when the knight lands on f5, our bishop slides back to f2. Castle first and that retreat to e3 is no longer available; the small developmental detail decides how smoothly the game runs.
The knight comes to f5, and the bishop drops to f2, first overprotecting the d4 pawn and, much later, eyeing a route into Black's position.
A bishop maneuver to h4 and f6 is a common infiltration, especially against a fianchetto with a bishop fianchettoed to g7.
We castle and keep developing. The h5 push is typical for this structure.

h5 does prevent g4, but it creates major dark-square weaknesses — notice the outpost on g5. That doesn't mean we leap there now; a knight to g5 lets Black trade and fill the holes. Later, though, g5 becomes a transit square, and a plan of trading on f5 and swinging the bishop to h4 hands our queen a swarm of juicy kingside outposts. With the center closed we have time — the position simply doesn't change fast.

A knight to a3 is a dead-end after a6, so instead the b1 knight goes to d2 — toward the center, going nowhere in particular yet, a Frankfurt-airport move you never regret. Remember, closed positions offer two broad plans: arrange your pieces to blast the center open, or maneuver on a flank.

Black plays a queen to b6. Here's our plan: rip the whole thing open and bank on our more active pieces handling the chaos better. Not a capture on c5 — that just hands Black space and the e3 square. Instead c4, building a pawn box that guarantees the center will open, perhaps after first eliminating Black's only active piece with a capture on f5.

c4 it is — and we can delay the capture on f5, playing it a little later. And we're not afraid of losing b2: when you've castled on the opposite wing a single b-pawn almost never matters, and here our queenside stays intact — Black can't unravel it the way a b2-then-c3 collapse would.

The queen grabs b2, but it creates no threats and doesn't stop our central agenda. Trying to trap it with a queen to a4 and a rook to b1 fails to a strong resource, and we lack the queenside firepower anyway — so we keep our focus in the center and press to open it.

We start with a move we know is good — capturing on d5. If Black doesn't recapture, the pawn marches to d6 and it's horrific for him, so he'll take back, and then a capture on f5 to wreck his structure is the idea.
Black recaptures on d5, and we should be tempted to grab the knight on f5 — giving up our light-square control hurts, but it's a price well worth paying.
So we capture on f5, taking the knight, while we still can, trading our good bishop to shatter Black's kingside pawns.
Black recaptures with the g-pawn, and now we complete the opening of the center.

We finish it with a capture on c5 — the center is now fully open, so we shift from luxurious positional play to hunting tactics. Black still hasn't developed his queenside, and we've invested a pawn, so we must hit the gas.
Black recaptures on c5. Only a couple of moves stand between him and consolidating that extra pawn, so we accelerate — and a bishop to d4 catches my eye, x-raying the rook.

The bishop to d4 hits the queen, centralizes beautifully, and prepares an e6 discovery against the rook — good as a plan and good as a plain developing move. It also shoos away that b2 queen, which was cramping our coordination.
Black shuffles the queen to a3, but our reply to almost anything here is e6 — and our opponent is defending this fantastically, making us work.
e6 is nearly automatic: without it, Black plants a knight into e6 and keeps the center closed.
Black plays a rook to g8 — and that, I think, is the decisive mistake.
Because now, without a second thought, we capture on f7, dragging the king out into the open.

The king is forced to f7 — f6 was the only survival try. Now the firepower tells: a knight to e5 with check, and lines flow, though a queen grab on h5 with check isn't yet mate because the king slips to d8.
A knight to e5 with check. Black could try the king to g6, using the king itself as a defender, but there's no reason to overcomplicate — the knight to e5 is clean.

The king walks out to e6. This looks like hara-kiri for Black. One pitfall for us is a rook to e1 — there's a knight jump to e4 in reply, and if the king ever steps to d6 a knight to c4 forks king and queen. No need for any of that: the simplest move is to capture the h-pawn, not for the pawn but to route the queen toward f7.

The queen takes h5, Black defends with a rook to f8, and the queen checks from h6 — the whole point being to prevent a bishop to f6. Compare your checks: two similar-looking checks rarely do the same job.
The rook is driven to f6, and remember — even mid-attack you're allowed to win material. Players fixate on delivering mate; here the rook sits under the bishop's x-ray.
A queen to g7 — using the weakness of Black's king to go after his pieces, because a king so exposed forces the defenders onto vulnerable squares.
Black finds the only move, a queen to b4, holding things together; a queen check on g8 and the king to d6 leaves us with a beautiful win to find.

A knight to f3 is what I like — it gives away nothing, prepares a knight to g5, and safely defends the bishop. A resilient defender makes you work, but at most levels the position collapses in a couple of moves.
Crucially, we've sacrificed nothing — it's plus eleven. If Black plays a knight to e4 to take the sting out of a knight to g5, the top computer move is a wonderfully quiet one.
Just a rook to c1 — bringing a piece into the attack and cutting the king off from its escape. These quiet inclusions are the moves people won't make when attacking, yet they decide the game.

The rook to c7 — its added presence overwhelms Black's defense.

tree.intro: Let's walk through the Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon. Watch the ideas as the moves play out.
tree.outro: That's the heart of the Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon.

node.idea: My recommendation is the Accelerated Dragon. White surprises with c4 — think of it as an English where White plays c4, we play c5, and White plays e4. Its drawback jumps out: White has created a massive hole on d4 — a square no pawn can ever defend, since the c- and e-pawns have advanced past it.

This gives our knight a potential outpost on d4 — but a hole existing doesn't mean occupy it at once. We start with the knight to c6, not to play the knight to d4 next: it's too early, with nothing else developed.
The knight to f3 would just knock a d4-knight off. It's the long-term weakness that costs White later. We also get a massive diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.
We play g6 — though in a classical game I'd prefer e6 or the knight to f6, since g6 allows White to transition to main lines.
The drawback of g6: it allows d4 — after d4, c takes d4, knight takes d4, we transpose to the Maroczy Bind Accelerated Dragon. Since we're emphasizing openings, I wouldn't mind. White plays d3.
After the bishop to g7, we're flat-out better: great pieces, dominating the dark squares, and White's light bishop is now a big pawn.

The knight to c3. We develop normally. It's self-evidently good to trade our light bishop for White's f3-knight — visualize it gone: our control of d4 increases, and we can contemplate the knight to d4, though White can still trade it with the dark bishop or the c3-knight, both awkward.
The best way to threaten that trade is d6 — a normal developing move I like more than the knight to f6, which I'll delay. White plays the bishop to e3.
We develop the bishop to g4, continuing to clamp d4, trading a piece that controls it — classic positional chess.
The bishop to e2. Do we take on f3 or wait? It doesn't matter — both are good.
I'll eliminate the knight while we can, capturing on f3 — the drawback of waiting is that the knight could move away.
White recaptures, capturing on f3.

The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto the dark bishop, then carve a square for the g8-knight with e6, keeping the bishop unobstructed. The e6 pawn is an asset, controlling d5 and f5 — a toothy central construction.
White can play the knight to b5 — a paper tiger, chase it with a6. And we don't worry about weakening the d6 pawn, well protected by the queen. The bishop to g5.

The break is b5, prepared with a6 — an unassuming move. And b5 is already available: after b5, c takes b5, a takes b5, queen takes b5, the knight jumps to d4, ruining the kingside structure or even reaching c2. The moment a rook appeared on e1, I am eyeing the knight jumping to c2. This a6-b5 plan is universal in anti-Sicilians.

We don't rush the knight to d4, keeping it for the right moment. White plays h3, doing nothing about b5. I like the knight to d4 first: then the bishop has only d1, since after the bishop to g4 we chase with h5; then b5 virtually traps the queen — c2 and b3 are covered by the knight, and if the queen goes to a3, b4 forks. b5 immediately is slightly inaccurate, letting the queen drop to d1.

After b5, the queen to d1, the knight to d4, you no longer threaten the knight-takes-f3 check, so the effect is diminished. After the knight to d4, a strong player plays the queen to d1, White's only non-losing move — hard to find, since moving the bishop back seems natural. It's worth starting with the knight to d4, more flexible, testing White — being practical, not tricky.
a3 — fine with us, we continue the plan: expand on the queenside, open files.
Our queen is stuck in no man's land — it could go to b7 to x-ray b2, but I'm looking at White's king: the queen to g5, threatening the knight-f3 check, with a second idea of infiltrating to d2.
The rook to a2 doesn't defend the knight-f3 threat.
The knight to f3 with check.

The bishop to g7, developing and pressuring the d4-knight down the long diagonal.
White develops the bishop to e3 — the main line.
So we keep it uniquely Accelerated by developing the knight to f6 first — not pushing any central pawns yet, maybe not for several more moves.

White plays the queen to d2 — a not-especially-good sideline; the main is the bishop to c4. In any Dragon setup, once the queen leaves d1, consider the knight to g4: trading it for White's dark-squared bishop leaves our Dragon bishop uncontested. After the knight to g4 the bishop can't move — it would drop the twice-attacked d4-knight — though White can take on c6 and shift the bishop to d4.
We castle. And we don't play d6, which would let White transition to the Dragon with f3 — keeping the pawn on d7 means we can later strike with d5 in one move.

White castles queenside. Now the king and queen are aligned, so we recalculate the knight to g4: if White takes c6 and plays the bishop to d4, we have the bishop to h6, pinning the queen. White blocks with f4 — but then the pawn to e5 is winning.
The knight to g4 — hitting the f4-pawn, threatening the capture on f4, and attacking the d4-bishop: a simple double attack that costs White at least a piece.
White takes on c6.

We recapture with the b-pawn, ruining White's structure and opening the b-file — with White castled queenside that often spells immediate doom. The queen to b6 hits f2, which the g4-knight also attacks; the pawn to e5 chasing the bishop is another plan.
White plays the bishop to d4.
We respond instantly with the bishop to h6, pinning the queen.
White plays the pawn to f4, walking right into the losing line.

The pawn to e5 — the crusher. With the queen pinned, the f4-pawn can't move, so it's as if it isn't there and e5 wins. White's best is to take on e5 and decline the recapture, down a full piece. Then the attack is decisive: the c3-pawn becomes a battering ram shattering White's queenside cover, the queen to b6 threatens mate in one plus a check on e3, and the lobster-pincer mate with the queen reaching a3 finishes it — first opening the centre with d5 so the king finds no relief, and connecting the rooks with the bishop to g4 to bring a rook to d8.
The bishop to c5, closing the diagonal — which takes a lot of the fun out of the Dragon; a very popular line where White is considered better.
The rook to e8 — Black often sacrifices the exchange here, though Giri recommends this relatively rare rook move.

node.idea: White plays the bishop to e2 — a peaceful line. It's not bad, but it lets Black equalize.

White castles. There's a specific reason White usually puts the bishop on c4 in the Accelerated — to stop the freeing break we're about to make.
The pawn to d5! We exploit the drawback of White's setup — and in the Accelerated, if you get a good version of d5 in, you solve all your opening problems.
White captures on d5. Our pieces are active and it's equal — White isn't worse with accuracy, but can drift worse if careless.

White plays the bishop to d4, and it's equal — so we must manufacture winning chances. One option is the knight takes c3, forcing a pawn recapture that ruins White's queenside, though both structures suffer. A more circumspect idea is the bishop takes d4, the queen recaptures, then the queen to b6, forcing a queen trade on our terms to fix the structure — though that may just draw.
We choose the knight takes c3 — it creates more imbalance and is the simpler move.
White recaptures with the bishop, also wanting to trade bishops.
That's fine — we take, ruining White's pawn structure.
White plays the queen takes d8 — not a good move: it hands us the d-file and plays for a draw.
We recapture on d8, and White recaptures the bishop. He's playing for a draw — now we devise a strategy to play for the win.
The rook to d2 is tempting but not as good as it looks — the bishop to d3 would trap it. Instead the bishop to f5, developing with tempo and hitting c2.
White plays the bishop to f3.

We calculate: the bishop takes c2, and if the bishop takes c6, the rook to c8 skewers the bishop and the pawn. We absolutely take — and a bonus is that White can no longer swing a rook to b1 or to d1, so our bishop is superb.
White plays the rook to e1. Our bishop is so strong we protect it at all costs, unless White chases it away properly.
We play the pawn to e6, defending it — the king to f8 was also fine and it barely matters.

White's big idea is to pin our rook and then pick off the bishop. The real problem isn't the bishop — it's that the c3-rook is undefended; if it were defended, the bishop could go anywhere. The most efficient, safe way is the rook to d7 and then c7.
The rook to d7. Objectively the rook to d2 may be better, but I don't want the headache of an unprotected rook. To beat a pin, either move the pinned piece — not possible here — or reinforce it.
White plays the bishop to e4.
The rook to c7 — the whole point of the last move: now the bishop is free to move.
Now the rook is defended by two rooks and White is in huge trouble. White tries the bishop to f3 to keep pieces on — so where do we place our bishop most accurately?
The bishop to a4 — it stops the rook coming to d1, denying White the open files, and it's invulnerable there; on f5 it could face g4 ideas.
We don't want the bishop on a square where it can be easily attacked.

White plays the rook to e2 — and the bishop to d1 is the crushing skewer; if White defends, we trade into a trivially winning pawn endgame. There the technique is: find White's weakness — the isolated h3-pawn — and tie down his king by marching ours toward h4, so his king is stuck near g2 and h2. Then advance our pawns carefully, avoiding a swiss-cheese structure: don't push into an e4 or f4 fix. Start with the pawn to e5, then f5 and g5, and the king takes the route to the h-file — the rare exception to centralizing the king. A patient, winning grind.

node.idea: The bishop to c4 — a sharp Sozin-flavoured try that stares down f7. We simply carry on developing.
We castle, and note what we're deliberately NOT doing: pushing the pawn to d6 yet. Holding it back preserves maximum flexibility for what comes next.

The knight steps back to e2 — a poor choice, because it abandons the strong central d4-square and does nothing active. And here's a reflex worth burning in: whenever White keeps a bishop on e3, always keep one eye on it. There is a way to challenge White at once. We could play the calm d6 — perfectly fine — but if we want to be maximally testing, a sharper idea is waiting.
The knight jumps to g4, leaping at the bishop on e3. If the bishop moves, we get to hit f2 and b2 at the same time — and with the c-pawn already traded off, that double attack has real teeth.
White slides the bishop to g5 rather than the tempting retreat to d4, which would just drop the bishop. Now the second pattern to know is armed: the queen sortie.
The queen swings out to b6, forking the pawns on f2 and b2. It carries risk — our light-squared bishop still isn't out — but the pressure should tell.
White castles, choosing to hold f2 and let the other pawn go. A garden-variety double attack: one of the two pawns is going to fall.
We capture on b2. The key question before ever taking like this is always the same — can the queen be trapped? Here, no chance.

White chases with the rook to b1, and the queen simply steps to a3. That's the whole safety net: from b2 the queen had a3, and beyond it a5 and c5 — too many routes to be caught in a single move. That is exactly the check to run before snatching a pawn: list the queen's escapes, and ask whether any one move takes them all away.

White's best try — the knight leaps to d5, generating real pressure, so we must stay careful. Even so, it's hard to see much for the pawn; our position is solid. To consolidate we want the queen back — either to c5, or to d6. But the queen-to-d6 has to be calculated: it steps off the a3-e7 diagonal, dropping the guard on e7, and then the knight crashes in with a check on e7, forking the king and the knight on c6 — losing material. So d6 is out, and c5 is the safe route.

The knight comes back into the centre to e5 — retreating from a loose square, hitting the bishop, and centralising, all at once. And crucially the queen still guards e7 for now: if White probes with a rook to b3, the c5-square is always waiting for the queen.

White tucks the bishop back to b3, out of harm's way. Now we diagnose what's blocking full consolidation. We'd love to play d6 to free the light-squared bishop — but d6 cuts the queen's defence of e7 and drops that pawn. So d6 has to wait.

Instead we start kicking. Trying to fianchetto with b6 wouldn't cure the real disease — White's two strong pieces on d5 and g5. We need to chase at least one away, maybe both later with a well-timed e6. The pawn to h6 first — the most flexible poke, keeping options open depending on where the bishop runs.
The bishop retreats to h4, staying on the pin — and where it lands decides our next step.
We keep coming — the pawn to g5, chasing the bishop away entirely. This unburdens our position and lets us consolidate on our own terms.

The bishop drops to g3. Now d6 finally works — e7 is covered well enough. We could also try e6, but combining g6 and e6 leaves too many dark-square holes, so there's no rush to chase the d5-knight yet.

So the pawn to d6 at last — solid and freeing. And if White tries the knight to c7, there's simply no follow-up: the rook steps to b8 and nothing comes of it. That jump only bites if a rook were sitting on e8, which it isn't.
White plays the correct plan — the pawn to h4, prying open our king. This won't be an easy game.
We finally develop the light-squared bishop to g4. Honest admission: White's h4 is stronger than it first looks — this was underestimated.
White centralises the queen to d2 — a good move. Now we've got an interesting resource: the queen to a5, trying to force the queens off.

The queen to a5, offering the trade. There's a tactical wrinkle — White has the check on e7 — but calculate one step further: after the knight takes e7 with check, the king steps to h7, and now we hit two things at once, White's queen and the checking knight, so the queens come off. We hand back the extra pawn, but the mating danger evaporates.
White declines and lifts the queen to e3 — music to the ears, because now the check on e7 no longer bites: that knight is tied to defending White's own queen, so the moment it moves, the queen falls.
So the queen to c5, again pressing for the exchange and eyeing White's queen.
White sidesteps to d2. No matter — our queen is beautifully centralised while White's is tied to the knight. That means we can get on with the plan: e6.
The pawn to e6, kicking the d5-knight. A strange, tense structure — the pawn-grab has led to a real fight, and if the knight retreats to e3 there's a very pretty resource waiting.
The knight goes to e3. And here's that resource — not a gimmick, it genuinely does something.

The bishop drops in to f3! It's untouchable thanks to the fork, and the point is plain: we're hitting the e4-pawn. With such a strong knight on e5 backing the operation, that pawn is hard to hold — normally a capture on c5 would break the pin, but the other knight just recaptures and the bishop stays immune.
White grabs on g5.
We have to recapture on g5 — otherwise our whole kingside is shattered.
White captures our centralised knight, the bishop landing on e5.
We recapture on e5 with the other knight — all according to plan.
The knight to g3, a good defensive try. Suddenly our f3-bishop could become a liability — if White's queen ever steps aside, the bishop can be taken. Time to think about shoring it up.

The pawn to g4 — solidifying the bishop, and more than that, preparing to sacrifice it: if White captures on f3, our knight recaptures and gets anchored by this very pawn. The deeper idea is to bring the dark-squared bishop to h6 and crank up the pressure.
White finds a very strong move — the queen to c1. And now our f3-bishop really is trapped.
We carry on with the plan — the bishop to h6, pinning the knight and pouring heat onto White's position. The f3-bishop is lost, so we roll with it and turn it into fuel.
White takes the bishop, a pawn recapturing on f3.

And now the instructive choice — most players would recapture with the knight, but we take with the pawn. This f3-pawn is a far more dangerous attacker: it jams White's position and becomes an anchor point for mating ideas. We're down a piece for two pawns, but White's king is the one in danger.
White unpins with the queen to e1. We have many ways to improve.
The king to h7 — stepping off the g-file so the rook can pour down it into the attack.

White cracks under the pressure — the knight to c4, which simply hangs itself. But the beautiful point is that we don't need to take it. The first thing to notice isn't the loose knight — it's that White's pawn on f2 is now pinned, so it no longer guards the knight.
So the in-between move — the rook to g8, threatening the crushing capture on g3 with check. Once that knight vanishes, White's king stands utterly alone.
White's king shuffles to h2. We keep our eyes on the bigger prize, not the loose knight on c4.
The knight to g4 with check — crushing.

The king to h3. Now don't drown in the sea of winning moves — plan properly. The real target is getting the queen over to the kingside, ideally to h6. What's in the way? Our own bishop. So move the bishop first.
But we don't bury the bishop uselessly — the bishop to f4 keeps it in the attack while clearing the queen's route via g5 to h6.
White pushes the pawn to e5. And here we spot an even faster finish — the knight crashes in on f2 with check.
The knight takes on f2 with check and the game is essentially over. A rook lift to g5 was also winning, but this is the cleanest.

White slides the bishop to g5 rather than the tempting retreat to d4, which would just drop the bishop.
The knight jumps to g4, leaping at the bishop on e3.
The knight steps back to e2 — a poor choice, because it abandons the strong central d4-square and does nothing active.
We castle, and note what we're deliberately NOT doing: pushing the pawn to d6 yet.
The bishop to c4 — a sharp Sozin-flavoured try that stares down f7.
So we keep it uniquely Accelerated by developing the knight to f6 first — not pushing any central pawns yet, maybe not for several more moves.
White develops the bishop to e3 — the main line.
The bishop to g7, developing and pressuring the d4-knight down the long diagonal.
White plays the knight to c3 — the other main line, as opposed to the Maroczy Bind with c4.

node.idea: White develops the bishop to e3.
The bishop to g7 — the fianchetto, applying immediate pressure on White's centre down the long diagonal.

White plays the pawn to c3 — already a mediocre move. It reinforces the knight and takes some sting out of our bishop, but it doesn't develop anything, it robs White's own knight of the c3-square, and it leads to very passive development.
So the knight to f6 — no need to reinvent the wheel: knight out, castle, then d5, often without even needing d6.
White plays the bishop to b5 — and simply blunders a pawn.
No reason not to take — the knight captures on e4, and the mediocre opening is already bearing fruit.
White takes on c6 — moving the bishop twice to grab a knight that only moved once. Both recaptures are reasonable, but I like to prioritize piece activity over pawn structure.
We recapture with the d-pawn on c6 — up a pawn, it opens a line for the queen and frees our light-squared bishop onto a juicier diagonal. And we keep the two bishops as a unit.
White castles.
We castle too. The e4-knight is perfectly placed — undefended, but there's no way for White to fork it, and everything else is covered.

White plays the knight to d2. We could trade knights, but for spice we keep them on: White's d2-knight is passive with no prospects, while ours is central and flexible — we can even retreat it to f6 and reroute to g4 or d5.

So the knight goes back to f6 — a retreat in name only, redeploying toward an outpost on d5 or the strong g4-square, and keeping pieces on makes it harder for White to breathe. White jumps the knight to c4, where it feels a touch loose — the queen to c7 or d5 comes to mind.
We play the queen to c7, keeping the tension. This is a universal, very safe construction — the c6-pawn guards against knight jumps to b5 and d5, and the queen sits comfortably.
White plays the queen to f3, intending the bishop to f4 to hit our queen — something we can cut across with a bit of calculation.
The knight to d5 — centralizing and stopping the bishop to f4; the knight to g4 was also good. Now we're ready to push our central pawns.

White plays a rook to d1. We don't take the bishop — our central knight is a monster, defended by the pawn and blanketing the position. The theme is keeping the tension, not trading unless forced, and it's time to start the kingside plan of e5, f5, and e4. The pawn to h5 threatening the bishop to g4 is met simply by h3, so it's not worth the weakening.
So the pawn to e5 — kicking the d4-knight, with f5 and then e4 or f4 to ram our pawns down the board. Notice how vulnerable White's queen is compared to ours.

White retreats the knight to b3, and we push the pawn to f5. White's pieces are like unanchored bowling pins — we just keep rolling them back with our pawns, while our own pieces are well anchored, either far away or protected by a pawn.
White centralizes the other rook to e1. Our e5-pawn needs no more defence — it's going to e4.
The pawn to e4, gaining space.
White plays the queen to g3, offering a queen trade — which we could accept.
But we keep the tension and stay aggressive with the pawn to f4 — risky, and it loosens our e4-pawn, but it blunts White's pressure.
White plays the queen to h4. Now the c8-bishop has the square the f-pawn vacated, which also defends f5 — and White's queen is running short of squares.
We develop the bishop to f5 — not rushing, but keeping an eye on White's queen for a possible trap.

White plays the knight to d4 — a strong player, though not threatening anything. It might be worth bringing pieces to the kingside; the queen to f7 tempts, but it runs into the knight to d6, which I'd rather not face.
The core problem is White's pieces encroaching, so we push them back — the pawn to b6, kicking the c5-bishop and looking to dislodge a central knight, making it easier to manoeuvre.
White captures on f5. The downside for us: our c6-pawn loses the support of its neighbour and the queen is a little tied — but our position is active enough to handle it.
We recapture with the pawn on f5 rather than allow the capture of our fianchetto bishop. A nice pawn box — the king is slightly weakened, but nothing we can't deal with.
White plays the bishop to d4. Many players would look at our king and call it weak — but be concrete: White has no rook lift, our pawns cover the whole third rank.
Still, we tuck the king to h8, out of the crossfire — unworried by the pin, since the bishop trade is coming. And note the half-open g-file can favour US too: a rook to g8 targets White's f-pawn.
White finds the queen to g5 — a brilliant move.
The pawn to f3, targeting the g2-pawn and laying the groundwork for the classic pincer mate.
White pushes the pawn to g3. Now, what's the cleanest way to orchestrate the mate?
The rook to f6 — the pretty idea: lift the rook to h6 for mate, or begin with a queen sacrifice.
White plays the knight to e5.
And the rook to h6 — checkmate, with White's own rook on g1 blocking the king's only escape.

node.idea: White plays a knight to c3. Which reply depends on your Sicilian: Najdorf players play d6, Accelerated Dragon players play a knight to c6.
So a knight to c6, since we're playing the Accelerated Dragon here.
White plays a knight to f3 — we proceed expecting d4 next.
As Accelerated Dragon players, it's easy — we play g6, and if d4 comes we take and transpose straight into an Accelerated Dragon.
White plays d4.
We capture on d4.
And we fianchetto the bishop to g7 — our first Accelerated Dragon.

White plays a bishop to e3. The zen of this opening is to delay d6 — playing it early lets White transpose into the sharp mainline Dragon, and by holding off we deny White comfortable queenside castling.
So we develop the knight to f6 first, keeping the option to play d5 in one fell swoop.

White plays a3 — a sideline I've never seen, essentially a waste of time since we're not putting anything on b4. But we can't play d5 yet: before castling, a bishop to b5 pins our knight and threatens a capture on c6 and a bishop fork on e6.
So we castle kingside first — the rule of thumb is only play d5 after castling. Now we're ready to open the center and punish White for delaying.
White plays a bishop to c4 — and here's the center fork trick, a ubiquitous idea you cannot play the Accelerated without knowing. The precondition is a bishop on c4 (or, for Black, on c5).
We play a knight capture on e4 anyway — it looks like a blunder, but with the trick in hand it isn't.
White recaptures on e4, and we meet it with d5.
d5 re-forks the knight and bishop — that's where the name comes from — and we win the piece back. White can give the piece for a pawn, but here it isn't even easy for him to regain it.
If White plays a knight capture on c6...
...we recapture with the pawn, protecting d5 with our new c6 pawn — and White really pays for a3, because normally this arises with White already castled; keeping the king in the center burns him.

White plays a knight to g3. A very bad move now would be a bishop capture on b2 — we've already sacrificed a piece, so after we grab the rook White recaptures with the queen and we're left with rook and two pawns for two pieces, usually worse, and we've given up our precious fianchetto bishop.
So we simply recapture on c4 — now we're up a pawn.
White trades queens into an endgame.
We recapture on d8 — we'll still need good technique to finish in style.

White plays c3, closing off our bishop. With queens off, our king is safe — so no need to rush the c8 bishop out; the bigger fish is the b2 pawn. Our pawn on c4 deep-freezes it: b2 is backward with no path forward, a huge weakness on an open file.
So a rook to b8 — a move that begs to be played, needing no calculation. And a7 can't be taken.
White plays a rook to b1 — but a loose piece drops off, because the rooks aren't coordinated.
The move that ends it is a bishop capture on c3 with check.

tree.intro: Let's walk through the King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation. Watch the ideas as the moves play out.
tree.outro: That's the heart of the King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation.

node.idea: We meet the queen-pawn setup with the knight to f6; White stakes out c4 and d4, and we're heading into a King's Indian.
We fianchetto with g6, and White develops the knight to f3.
The bishop lands on g7, and White goes for the fianchetto too with g3 — one of the most respected tries against the King's Indian.
We reply with the classical d6.
White completes the fianchetto, the bishop settling on g2.
We castle, and White castles.
We pick the classical setup — the queen's knight to d7. Easy to learn, easy to understand, and what I play in my serious blitz.
White develops the bishop to g5, eyeing our knight — though the e7-pawn means it's no real pin.
The knight to d7 is at least as common as the knight to c6 here — c6 invites d5 with tempo, and d7 sidesteps that.
And the whole idea of the d7-knight is to prepare the e5 break.
So the bishop to g5 shows up — common at the lower levels, but not really threatening, since it isn't hitting anything it can win on f6.
We ask the bishop the polite question with h6.
White hands over the bishop pair, capturing on f6.
We recapture on f6 with the knight — flexibility. With White's dark-squared bishop gone, White brings the other knight to c3.
We carve open the long diagonal with c5.
White clamps the centre with d5 — now it's a Benoni structure, and that long diagonal is beautiful.
The bishop comes to f5, preparing the knight to e4 — a very standard maneuver.
White plays the knight to d2 to stop e4. It's a good move, but if White ever pushes e4, that d2-knight is left without a clear home.
We play a6, planning to drop the bishop calmly back to d7.
White grabs the centre with e4, and the bishop retreats to d7, ready for the classic Benoni break, b5.
White reroutes with the knight to f3, preparing to counter-strike with e5.
We stop it with the knight to g4, heading for the e5 outpost.
White pokes with h3, and the knight lands on e5, going for a trade.
White takes on e5, and we recapture with the bishop, capturing on e5 — this bishop is our main asset.
White lunges g4, doing nothing at all against our real plan of b5.
We push b5. Some would grab dark squares with g5 here, but that would be a serious mistake.
White takes on b5, and we recapture with the a-pawn, capturing on b5.
White brings the queen to d2, hitting the h6-pawn.
Rather than g5, we keep piling on with b4.
White retreats the knight to e2.
The bishop swings to b5 — indirectly defending h6, since grabbing that pawn would now achieve nothing.
White lifts the rook to e1, reinforcing the threat.
We tuck the bishop back to g7, which also stops f4 coming with tempo.
White plants the knight on f4. Back to the queenside: c4 is tempting, but it would drop the b4-pawn.
So we prepare it and beef up the queenside with the queen to a5.
White throws in h4.
Now we step on the gas with c4.
White pushes h5.
We could close the kingside with g5, but there's no need yet — instead we play c3.
White captures on c3.
The greedy move is to grab material, but we recapture on c3 with the b-pawn — very much in the King's Indian spirit.
White drops the queen to c2.
Now we shut the kingside with g5 so our king never gets pried open.
White reroutes the knight to d3. Time for the final stage on the queenside.
There's the quiet bishop to a4, but the Soviet way is the queen to a4, offering the trade.
White takes, and we recapture with the rook, capturing on a4 — the queen trade itself is our weapon, and White's position collapses.
White scrambles the knight back to c1.
The passed pawn marches to c2.
White tries the knight to b3, but the rook on a1 is now trapped.
We collect the exchange, capturing on a1 with the bishop.
White recaptures on a1 with the rook.
We bring the other rook in — to a8, not c8 — forcing White's knight back to c1.

children.idea: White's rook retreats to c1, and we snatch the pawn, capturing on a2 with the rook — the rook to b4 and b1 was cleanest, but this wins too.
White's king steps to h2.
We swing the back rook down to a3, doubling on the third rank.
White tries the knight to d4, and the bishop comes to d3, guarding the c2-pawn.
White lurches the knight to b5 — a serious inaccuracy.
We simply capture on b5 with the bishop; White has blundered the knight.
White plays f3.
The bishop returns to d3.
White's king wanders to g3, and we plant a rook on a1.
White grabs the c-pawn, and we recapture with the bishop, capturing on c2 — up two full rooks now.
White's king shuffles to f2.
We double the rooks again, the back one to a2.
White's king goes back to g3, and the bishop snaps the pawn, capturing on e4.
White tries the bishop to h3.
We finish it — the rook captures on f3, checkmate. A classic, smooth King's Indian win.

Black pins with the bishop to g4. We must move the queen — to d2, or the interesting e1 to drag it toward the kingside.
The queen goes to d2. I avoid e1 because it runs into the knight rerouting to d4, and we want c2 guarded; from d2 the queen can also swing to f4 later.
Black jumps the knight to d4 — but it no longer carries a threat and hands us a free tempo.
We play the cryptic bishop to e5, pressing the knight on d4 — hoping Black obliges with the knight from e7 to c6.
Black finds the queen to h5 instead — a different, even stronger way of hitting our e5-bishop.
We drop the bishop back to g3 — where it was headed anyway, off the awkward c7-square and out of tactical trouble.
Black plays the knight to g6. My trick failed — yet it half-worked, because moving that knight has the same effect I was after.
Here's why I wanted that knight off e7: it guarded d5. Now we plant the knight on d5 and start building central pressure.
We were eyeing c3 next — but Black finds the knight to e2, a really nasty shot I missed. The bishop to f2 would defend, but ...Bd6 keeps the pressure; our emergency resource is the queen to e1.
So the queen to e1, forced — Black is playing superbly; that knight leap completely escaped me.
The knight takes on g3 with check — it was a mating threat — and we recapture with the queen. The trade actually helps us: Black has thinned his own attack, and now h3 is coming.
Black brings a rook to d8, setting a threat. We have two pawns for the piece — consolidate and we hold real chances.
The threat was ...Bd6, skewering the queen with mate to follow — so h3 must come at once, blunting it; if Black tries ...Bd6 anyway, we simply take the bishop on g4.
Black retreats the bishop to e6. Our sole trump is the central pawn mass Black doesn't have, so we must expand there.
We play c3, preparing to roll the centre with d4 and later e4–e5.
Black plays the bishop to d6. We're in deep trouble — ...Qe5 next is a serious problem.
We try the queen to f2 — a long shot, hoping to bait a sacrifice on h3.
Black takes the bait, sacrificing on h3.
We recapture, gxh3 — and I can't quite see where Black's mate is.
Black checks on h3, our king goes to g1 — and ...Nh4 is a bolt from the blue, threatening ...Nf3 with check and a mating net.

But there may be a defence. The knight lands on h4 threatening ...Nf3, which works only by pulling our queen off f2 — so we sidestep the queen. And here c3 pays off: a bishop to c5 now would allow d4, so if ...Nf3 comes we take it with the rook and keep control of h2. Black has a perpetual for a draw if he wants it — I'd gladly take that; what would truly worry me is a slow strengthening move like ...Re8.

node.idea: We play the knight to f6, angling for the Stafford.
But the knight to c3 sidesteps it — no Stafford now. You can play d5 here for an interesting game, and the bishop to c5 might transpose to the Stafford.
We try the bishop to c5, Eric Rosen style, hoping to goad a gambit.
He plays the bishop to c4 — so we'll have to play conventionally, but we'll make it interesting.

If we castle and he takes, there's no Stafford left — he's close to castling. So we either play the knight to c6 into a Four Knights, or d6; it doesn't much matter, so we start with d6 to defend the e5 pawn.
White castles. Now, to make it hard for him to develop, how do we add some spice?
The bishop to g4 — because if we play the knight to c6 first, knowing his style he'll play h3 and we'll regret it, so we squeeze this in while we can. He'll probably retreat to e2.
Now we play the knight to c6, threatening the knight to d4.

The bishop to e3. A classic line. The knight to d4 is possible but less strong with the bishop on e3, since he can take with the bishop and keep his structure. Against boring players, keep the tension — give them rope and force decisions.

The classic way to make White decide is to drop the bishop back to b6, avoiding his taking on c5 and ruining our structure — and if he takes now, a takes b6 gives us doubled pawns that don't matter, plus the a-file, which is great.
Make these players think, and they'll do something irrational or panic. h3.
We drop the bishop to h5 — he'll probably contemplate g4 for a while; if he plays it, we consider a sacrifice on g4.
I don't think the time's right for the sac — not enough there — so we keep the bishop. He plays the king to h2, a weird move; maybe planning the rook to g1 and g4.
We just castle — no point doing anything wild.

The queen to d2. Now I see his idea: the king went to h2 so that after the bishop takes f3, g takes f3 keeps his king off the open file, and he can play the rook to g1 and attack down the g-file — even with a ruined structure, he gets the file.
Does that warrant not taking on f3? No — the bishop takes f3, capturing on f3, creates such damage on his kingside that it's worth it, as long as we're careful.

He recaptures, capturing on f3. The weaknesses he's created are permanent, so it's worth it if we manage the open g-file. Two things: start kingside operations, moves like the knight to h5, and balance that with some prophylaxis.
The greater priority is to stake a claim on the kingside so he doesn't run circles over us — so the knight to h5, getting the wheels turning.
The rook to g1 — a pin. Many people reflexively play the king to h8, but that tempo could matter against a skilled attacker. Where's the queen doing more, on f6 or h4? Only one creates a threat.
The queen to f6 — on h4 it does nothing, since we've no light-squared bishop to hit h3; on f6 it's active.
The rook to g4, ignoring the attack on f3 — this guy's legit, gone from passive to aggressive in a snap.
As the Russian expression goes, having said A you must say B — putting the queen on f6 and NOT taking on f3 makes no sense, so the queen takes f3, capturing on f3.

The rook to g1, doubling — now the threats on g7 are serious. One more move and he creates insurmountable threats, probably a sacrifice; g6 doesn't solve it, and he could sack on g6 via the pin. So now's the time.
The king to h8 — the problem is the g-file, not his bishop. The king to h8 is the better move.
The knight to d5 is good — this guy's very legit; I'll play faster. We keep attacking; our king is very safe.
We need spice on the kingside — open files, something to join this lonely queen. So f5 — gutsy play by both of us.
He takes, capturing on f5. With my queen so dominant and the knight on h5 defending g7, I'm optimistic about the attack.
The rook takes, capturing on f5.

The rook to g2 — this seems like capitulation of his attack, which I like; it means he doesn't know what to do and is milking my clock. Now g7 is protected; we want to triple, with the knight to d4 and the rook to f8 coming.
The rook to f8, continuing to pile pieces on the kingside — no need to change strategy.
He takes, capturing on b6 — you have to take.
We recapture, capturing on b6, checking for intermediate moves first — nothing there.
The bishop to e6 — a very advanced idea I'll admit I missed: if we move the rook, he plays the bishop to g4 and wins a piece. So we'll have to sac the exchange.

tree.intro: Let's walk through the Philidor Defense. Watch the ideas as the moves play out.
tree.outro: That's the heart of the Philidor Defense.

node.idea: We open e4, Black replies e5, and we head for our Four Knights Scotch.
The knight goes to f3.
Black develops to c6. A bonus of this system: you needn't learn a separate line against the Petrov — the knight to c3 covers it, saving work.
We play d4 as usual — with Black so passive, why not.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture with the knight.
The knights come off and our queen recaptures on d4 — Black often trades everything here, but our queen sits beautifully.

Black develops the knight to f6. Note: a later ...c5 is no threat — it would only weaken d6 badly and hand us the d5-square as an outpost for a knight. Don't fear your queen being attacked; it isn't inherently dangerous.
We develop the bishop to g5, natural and strong — and since our queen has already left d1, castling long is on the cards.
Black plays the bishop to e7. The principled path is to castle queenside and then steamroll on the kingside and in the centre.

We check with the bishop on b5. Black will block with ...Bd7 and we trade the light-squared bishops — excellent positionally: d5 grows even weaker, and with the light bishops gone nothing guards it, so we can take the f6-knight whenever we like and plant a knight on d5.

node.idea: Black plays d6 — the Philidor.
Against the Philidor we strike with d4. It's strong because ...d6 has left Black undeveloped and boxed in his own bishop.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture with the knight on d4. Those concessions mean we open the centre to exploit them.
Black develops the knight to c6.
We simply develop the knight to c3 — no need to rush the d4-knight; once he trades it off, our queen will be perfectly safe.
Black trades on d4 and we recapture with the queen — safe, because with no knight left on b8 there's no ...c-pawn or ...Nb8 tempo to chase it.
Black develops the bishop to d7. A caution: ...c5 to hit the queen is a classic mistake here — attacking the queen isn't automatically a good thing.
We continue with the bishop to c4, pressuring f7. The queen needs no move; we're happy to provoke ...c5, which would permanently weaken the d5-square.
Black develops the knight to e7; we castle.
Black attacks the queen with the knight to c6.
We tuck the queen back to d1 — Qd5 would walk into ...Be6, Qd3 into ...Ne5, and we don't want to give up our bishop. Sometimes you retreat, and it costs nothing when your pieces are this active.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
We swing the knight to the d5 outpost — a beautiful square. We could take the bishop at our leisure, but the knight is so strong we'd rather make him be the one to take it.
Black castles.
We grab more central space with f4 — not necessarily what I'd play myself, but a lesson in how to attack.
Black plays the bishop to e6. Development isn't finished — a good moment to maneuver.
The bishop looks awkward on d2, but it's a maneuver heading for the long diagonal — not b3, which would weaken it.
Black lunges the knight to a5, hitting our bishop.
We snap off the knight, the bishop landing on a5.
Black plays b6, attacking the bishop.
We slot the bishop onto c3 — the long diagonal we were aiming for all along — a clean piece up.
Black hits our knight with c6.
Rather than move the attacked knight, we set threats — the queen to d4, forming a battery with the bishop down the long diagonal toward g7.
Black grabs the knight, a pawn recapturing on d5 — but that opens the long diagonal straight to g7.
The queen crashes into g7 — checkmate.

node.idea: Black develops the knight to f6 and we bring ours to c3.
Black develops the bishop to e7. There are several good setups — the bishop to f4 with the queen to d2 — but a nastier one that flies under the radar is to fianchetto with g3.
We play g3 — the fianchettoed bishop and the e4-pawn team up to make it very hard for Black to break with ...d5.
Black castles.
We complete the fianchetto with the bishop to g2.
Black plays the classic ...c5 — but it's a positional error: it leaves the d6-pawn backward and, above all, weakens the d5-square. Now, where should our knight go? We want it working efficiently.
The knight to f5 allows ...Bxf5, a trade I don't want, so we play the knight to e2 — from there it heads to f4 to control d5.
Black develops the knight to c6.
No need to rush the knight to f4 — first we complete development and castle.
Black pins with the bishop to g4.
We play h3 to chase the bishop — f3 would work but we'd rather not weaken ourselves.
Black captures on e2.
We recapture with the knight, not the queen — the queen would walk into ...Nd4 with tempo. And we still deny ...d5: we hold three defenders against two attackers on that square.
Black plays the queen to b6. Our plan: reroute the knight to f4, and restrict Black's c6-knight.
We play c3, clamping down on the c6-knight's advance squares.

Black's knight to e5 is aimless. Rather than rush f4, we improve patiently: the queen to c2 defends b2, connects the rooks and prepares a rook to d1 reinforcing d5; then b3 to shoo the knight when we choose, the bishop to e3 x-raying the queen, and even c4 to clamp d5 harder — unafraid of the d4-square, since bishop and rook cover it. Keep turning the screw; under steady pressure, opponents buckle.
