node.idea: But I like starting with the bishop to c4 — incredibly tricky, and it sets an immediate trap: Philidor players are disconcerted when White doesn't play d4. I learned this from a Kasparov game; unlike his d3 Italian route, we'll follow up with d4.
Black develops the bishop to e7.
First we finish queenside development with the knight to c3, then we castle or play d4. The move order barely matters, as long as d4 arrives in good time.
Black develops the knight to f6.
This is as good a moment as any — the pawn to d4, opening the centre.
Black captures on d4 — still theory.
We recapture, the knight taking on d4.

Black castles — and now beware the universal center fork trick: the knight takes e4, then the pawn to d5 forks two of our minor pieces. It's not fatal — dropping the bishop to d3 keeps the bishop pair, three minors against three — but trading our e4-pawn for Black's d6-pawn is a bad deal: it opens Black's bishop and our whole edge rests on superior central control. We avoid it not with f3, which is weakening and we're not castled, but simply by moving the bishop.

The bishop to b3 — not d3, because if we wanted d3 why go to c4 at all? We developed to c4 to stay on this diagonal. The pawn there may look loose for a move or two, but we can defend it many ways after castling, and Black can't attack it effectively.

Black plays the pawn to a6, preparing to expand with b5. A reminder: don't reflexively meet a6 with a4 — sometimes you want to invite b5 and then answer with a4, shattering the chain. But here allowing b5 lets Black meet a4 with the pawn to c5, chasing the knight, then c4, locking our bishop out in a very concrete, tactical struggle.
And I'm not in the mood for something that concrete this early — so the pawn to a4, the direct prophylactic that stops b5. The pawn to a3 was possible, but a4 is the cleaner prevention.
Black develops the bishop to d7.
We continue with castling — unafraid of c5.
Black develops the knight to c6.
So we keep improving as if nothing's happening — the rook to e1, a good general move to make before committing the bishop.
Black captures, the knight taking on d4.
We recapture with the queen.

Black centralizes the bishop to c6. White is clearly better — better pieces, better centre — but Black is rock-solid with no weaknesses, and it's hard to make progress against a position with no weaknesses. Be patient and methodical, and don't imagine you're winning just because you have more space. Now, where to put the bishop? The bishop to g5 looks natural, but...
I dislike the bishop to g5 because Black moves the knight and offers a bishop trade — and trades favour the cramped side, plus Black's e7-bishop is a dud. So the bishop goes to f4 instead.

Black plays the knight to d7 — a fine Philidor move, preparing both c5 and the bishop to f6; our bishop bites on granite, but at least our rooks are coordinated. So I'll preemptively move the queen off d4, or the bishop to f6 would come with tempo.
The queen to d2 — a prudent prophylactic that also prevents the bishop to g5 offering a dark-squared trade. With our space edge, we want to keep pieces on.

Black plays the knight to e5. A kingside attack — the rook lift to e3 and g3 — is tempting, but hard: Black has defenders and the knight can return to g6 to cover the g-file. Better to play in the centre, where our superiority is greatest, with a natural move that forces Black to part with a bishop.
The knight to d5 — it makes no concession, just piles on central pressure and forces Black to give up one of the bishops.
Black captures, the bishop taking on d5. This is different from avoiding trades earlier — here we remove Black's strongest piece, the well-centralized bishop, and gain the bishop pair.
We recapture with the bishop, hitting b7 — not with the pawn, which would leave our bishop complaining about its own structure.
And Black's bishop comes to f6 — but we've finally induced our first weakness: the d6-pawn is now backward, and a central weakness is easy to attack, with the follow-up moves flowing naturally.

We threaten to take on f8; if Black grabs the rook we promote with check, and all Black can do is delay mate. node.idea: e4, e5 — an open game. We've been leaning on the Danish Gambit lately, but let's switch it up.
A knight to c3 — the Vienna. It's a phenomenal opening for anyone below master strength, largely because Black players simply don't study this move.
And a bishop to c5 is already a little inaccurate — the very reaction the Vienna preys on.
The whole idea of the Vienna Gambit is to improve on the King's Gambit: develop the knight first, watch how Black sets up, and only then play f4 — so you're better placed to meet a capture on f4.
And it turns out the bishop on c5 does nothing to stop f4, which a lot of people don't realize.
So f4 anyway. The bishop on c5 doesn't prevent it.
Black takes on f4. This is the hot-button moment, because we have to reckon with a queen check on h4.
A knight to f3 is essential — you can't answer a queen check on h4 with g3 because the f4 pawn just captures it. The knight to f3 covers h4 and is the best move here.
Black plays d6, holding the center — and we still have to keep an eye on that queen check.
And here I play a knight to d4 — a genuine blunder that simply drops the knight. Damage-control time.

Black captures on d4 and we've backed ourselves into a corner — down a knight, with the queen check on h4 still looming. We can't meet g3 with a recapture because both our rook and the pawn would hang.
A queen to f3 begins the recovery: now, if the queen comes to h4 and we answer g3 and the pawns trade, both the rook and the pawn are defended.
Black captures on c3 to trade — but that's already a small win for us, because that bishop was a monster. When you're down a piece, the priority is development.
We recapture with the d-pawn on c3 — the fastest route to quick development. We'll castle long, since the kingside is already wrecked.
Black plays g5 to defend the f4 pawn — another subtle mistake, because we're castling queenside and if his king goes short he'll pay dearly for that advanced pawn.
A bishop to d2, prioritizing development and king safety so we can start attacking. It isn't pretty, but we need to castle as fast as possible.

Castling long is the fastest way to safety. I don't care in the slightest about the a2 pawn — if Black grabs it we play b3 and trap the bishop; when you're down a piece you can't fret over a single pawn.
Black plays a6. Now, the idea I taught last game: when there's a pawn chain, attacking its base can make the whole structure topple.
So h4 — striking the foot of Black's g5-f4 chain. Knock out the base and the whole thing collapses.
We take on g5 to make that foot collapse. I know Black wants a bishop to g4, pinning my queen to the rook, but we're ready to give the exchange to topple his kingside.
Black plays the bishop to g4, and we'll sacrifice another exchange to make his whole kingside cave in.
The queen captures on f4 — we have to preserve the queen while Black grabs the rook.
Black takes our rook, landing on d1, and now we choose what to capture — because something very cool happens here.

After we recapture on f6, Black's bishop is trapped: it retreats to h5, but we've opened the h-file and our rook covers that square. That's the kind of thing that just falls into your lap when you play aggressively and hunt for chances.
Black plays a bishop to c2 — this still isn't better for White if he defends correctly, and he isn't defending badly.
The king recaptures on c2. He's given the bishop for a pawn.

Now we act on our strong f6 pawn — a great anchor for our pieces. The question is what Black wants: he won't castle kingside, since we'd mate him at once, so he'll try to castle queenside via a queen to d7, and we must stop that. A bishop to g4 tempts, but it has a drawback.

So g3 first, preparing a bishop to h3 instead — the difference being that after a bishop to e2 and g4, Black's knight to e5 covers g4; routed through h3, the bishop is far better protected. Same number of moves, better result.
Black plays a knight to e5.
And we go to h3 with the bishop.

Black's knight comes to g6 — but he still can't get his queen out; his pieces are stuck in molasses. He hits our queen, so we move it to a square that keeps the f6 pawn defended — that pawn is a huge bargaining chip.

A queen to f5. Not a queen to e3, which drops the pawn; not to f3, where a knight back to e5 hits it again; and not to g5, where h6 harasses it. f5 also builds a battery — a queen to d7 could be mate.

The e-pawn, of course — so paradoxically, rather than a slow rook move first, just play e5 to clear it and free the e-file for the rook.

node.idea: And we answer with the traditional knight to f6. This is still very much theory.

f4 — the Vienna Gambit, hugely popular lately thanks to Levy's course and a wave of content. Every e5 player needs to know how to meet it. People confuse it with the King's Gambit, but the difference is the two knights already out on c3 and f6 — which means accepting the gambit is terrible, because White shoves the pawn to e5 and our knight has to slink back to g8.
So Black has only one good move: counter-strike in the center with d5. It fits the classic rule — when your opponent is pushing pawns on the flank and loosening his king, you hit back in the center.
White captures on e5.
And we recapture with a knight on e4 — common, well-known theory. Now White has two tries.
A knight to f3 is the old move.
We make a developing move and keep the knight on e4 — no trading on c3 unless forced. A bishop to c5 is a fine choice: it threatens a knight fork on f2 and guards that square.
This might look dumb, since we walk right into d4, letting White grab the center with tempo and chase the bishop — but there's a catch.

d4 exposes the a5-e1 diagonal, so we swing the bishop to b4. Yes, moving a piece twice breaks a rule, but White gave us license by pushing so many pawns — here quality of development beats speed. Now we pressure the knight from two directions and threaten a capture on c3 that would fork the king and rook, forcing White to defend.

A bishop to d2 is White's best, but then we capture it with our knight, keeping the bishop pair and continuing to press the center with a later c5. To my knowledge this is the best way to equalize against the knight-f3 Vienna.

We eliminate the bishop and White recaptures with the queen. Now several solid options: a bishop to g4, a bishop to e6, or c5 against d4. I want to keep it solid, and I especially don't want a bishop to f5, because a bishop to d3 trades off our light-squared bishop — and I want to preserve the bishop pair, a genuine asset.
So the light-squared bishop develops to e6 — solid, completing our development quietly, with c5 still available down the line.

Where should the bishop go? Most would drop it to a5 to keep the pin, but that's an inaccuracy — White plays b4, and after the bishop retreats to b6 it's hemmed in by White's pawns, and, crucially, c5 becomes nearly impossible.
So we drop the bishop back to e7 instead, keeping c5 alive. White can still push b4, but now it comes without tempo — so it carries no threat, and we can undermine it with our own pawns.
The classic undermining move is a5 against a b4 push.
Let's continue developing — we castle.

White castles, and we have a major choice. We can play c5, which I've praised, but we can also aim for the other break most people are reluctant to try: f6. The reason is that White's e5 pawn hangs over us like the sword of Damocles, clamping our pieces and cutting communication between the flanks.

The best way to prepare f6 is to develop the knight — but to d7, not c6, so we keep c5 in reserve and the knight covers f6. It slightly loosens d5, but White can't pile on it, and we can always defend with c6.
We could build a little pawn chain with c6 if needed, so d5 is no worry. White plays a knight to d1.
White is probably rerouting the knight to e3, but that doesn't stop f6 — now is the perfect moment to push it and undermine e5. If White doesn't capture, we take on e5 ourselves.

White recaptures on f6, but that leaves the e5 pawn isolated — it loses the support of d4. Between the recaptures, a rook to f6 is awkward, so it's a knight or bishop capture: the knight recapture heads for the fine central e4 square, and though it allows a knight to g5, that's harmless — we drop the bishop to d7 and chase with h6.

So we recapture on f6 with the knight — the clearest path to a good position, always seeking the best square for a piece. Don't suffer from one-move-itis, fearing a move just because it makes a threat: moves aren't good simply because they threaten something.
White plays a knight to f2 — a good move; the position is fairly balanced. In these quiet, symmetric structures the best strategy is to find pieces that can be improved.
Our bishop can be repositioned from e7 to d6 — a better square, controlling more, discouraging a knight to e5, and clearing the e-file for a rook.
White mirrors with a bishop to d3. It's equal. We coordinate our rooks: a queen to d7, then a rook to e8, centralizing everything.
A queen to d7 — it defends the e6 bishop, so a rook to e1 no longer carries a threat and we can safely bring our own rook to e8. I've soured on c5, since White just meets it with c3.
White plays a rook to e1.
We do the same, a rook to e8 — totally equal. This is where 1700-level players often start to go wrong, unable to keep the tension without weakening.
White plays c3. Do we have a long-term plan? Not really — plans are overrated.

We play c6 to protect d5 and open the c7 square for our queen, so if a knight comes to g5 we needn't take it — we drop the queen aside. In open-center positions like this it's hard to form a plan, and you don't need one yet: both sides improve pieces until the confrontation comes.
White plays a bishop to c2 — a fine move eyeing a knight to d3. Our light-squared bishop is clearly worse than White's, so I want to trade it off.
A bishop to f5 — trading our worst piece for White's better one, and starting a direct confrontation: the rooks stare at each other and tension builds, fertile ground for tactics.
We recapture on e8 with the rook — the queen recapture would just drop the bishop. The pawn structure is dead symmetrical with the e-file open, so this will be a tough position to squeeze.
White captures on f5.
We recapture with the queen. These boring positions are exactly the ones you must learn to play without doing anything dumb — squeezing equal positions is an inevitable skill.

White plays a rook to e1, posing a decision: trade rooks, decline with a rook to f8 (which cedes the open file), or the option I like — block with a knight to e4, creating tactical tension. What bothers me is a queen to d3, hitting the undefended rook on e8.

We take the risk with a knight to e4, betting on a blunder. The key move behind everything is a rook to e6 — it solves our one problem, keeping the knight on e4 safe by guarding e8, and it prepares a rook lift to h6, because the bishop already eyes h2 and if the f3 knight ever moves, h2 becomes a fatal weakness. After White's c4 I first looked at a clearance sacrifice, a bishop capture on h2, but the combination needs setting up. So we play g5, aiming to push g4 — that both weakens f2 and, by forcing the f3 knight away, weakens h2; and White's king is nearly out of defenders, so opening our own kingside is safe when nobody's around to exploit it. After g4 the f3 knight is paralyzed, because moving it drops the f2 knight, and White's king is in serious trouble. The finish: a bishop capture on h2 forces the king there, then g3 forks king and knight; after the pawns trade we lift a rook to h6, and a rook to h1 is mate that White can do nothing about, since the f2 pawn is defended twice. It's objectively winning — pick the simple win over the beautiful one.

node.idea: We have Black against a strong opponent and play a very conceptual opening — the Caro-Kann, answering the king's-pawn with the pawn to c6.

White develops the bishop to d3 — the Exchange, one of the most reputable lines: very solid and London-like, with the bishop on d3, the pawn to c3, and the other bishop to f4. Black's setups all revolve around finding a home for the light-squared bishop, which, as in the French, often struggles for a good square — and if White plays h3, its development gets badly restricted.
So the soundest choice is the knight to f6 first, rather than the natural knight to c6 — and if White plays c3, we develop the bishop before it can be shut in.

The plan, step by step. The bishop pair is worth keeping active, so we take the light-squared bishop — the knight takes d3 with check, and the queen recaptures. Now the dark-squared bishop: e7 is too passive and c5 runs into the check on b5 that provokes the awkward knight to d7, so the right square is d6 — safe and eyeing the kingside. In an IQP position, whoever controls the square in front of the isolated pawn is better, and that's White on d4 — but our compensation is the bishop pair in an open position with fine coordination. If White plays the bishop to g5, we answer the pawn to h6, sacrificing the IQP for an open game and the two bishops. After the trade on f6 we recapture toward the centre — never with the g-pawn, which would wreck our structure. Then the rook swings to d8, an x-ray on the queen forcing it off the centre, and since White's queenside is undeveloped we pour on the initiative: the bishop to f5, ignoring the b7-pawn, chasing the queen around — the queen has almost no squares, and there's a recurring bishop-h2 back-rank motif because we still control the luft square even after White's h3. The deepest idea is the bishop to c2 setting up the retreat bishop to d6 to trap the queen. When we finally win the extra piece, we convert cleanly: simplify with a rook trade, force the queens off with the queen to e6 while keeping the bishop attacking the knight, then the deep freeze — the pawn to b5 to freeze White's queenside pawns so the dark-squared bishop can pick them off, trade the light bishop for the knight, and mop up.

I'll play c3 — a move with a very good reputation among top GMs. It looks purely positional, reinforcing the pawn, but a big point is that a queen check on a4 is a major idea while the king sits on e8: White develops on the a4-e8 diagonal and pressures Black before he completes development.
Black plays c5. The main moves for us are a knight to e5 or a bishop to e3.

A bishop to e3 — a developing move that pressures c5 and threatens to win a pawn with a capture on c5. If Black takes on d4 we recapture with the bishop, and the structure resembles an Alapin Sicilian, where a bishop in the center can be very powerful.

Black plays a knight to d5. A capture on c5 now runs into a knight capture on e3: even with queens off, Black recaptures the pawn and leaves us a poor structure plus the bishop pair — so the c5 capture is out. And a bishop check on b5 is ineffective, since Black just plays a bishop to d7.

So this is the moment for a knight to e5 — centralizing, and preparing a bishop check on b5 and a queen check on a4, against which a bishop to d7 no longer works: we take on d7, and the bishop to b5 wins the queen.

tree.openingName: King's Indian Defense (vs Barry / Jobava London)
tree.intro: Let's walk through the King's Indian Defense (vs Barry / Jobava London). Watch the ideas as the moves play out.
tree.outro: That's the heart of the King's Indian Defense (vs Barry / Jobava London).

node.idea: White opens d4, and we play the King's Indian move-order, the knight to f6.
The knight to f3.
We fianchetto with g6, heading for a King's Indian — my real opening repertoire at this stage.
The knight to c3 — the entry to the Jobava London or Barry system.
We play d5 here to stop White from move-ordering us into a Pirc, which we're not playing in this speedrun.
The bishop to f4, and we've transposed into the Jobava London — the old name is the Barry system, specifically the setup against g6.
We complete our fianchetto, the bishop to g7 — all standard fare.
White plays e3.
We complete kingside development with castling.

White plays the bishop to e2 — a quieter, tamer, more positional treatment. There's a sharp, tactical way to play the Jobava London, connected with an early pawn push, but here White is playing it strategically and quietly.
Black has a million ways to disarm the Barry. I'll play solidly — starting with c6, shoring up the centre and in some lines preparing the queen to b6.
And White does play h4, combining two ideas: the bishop to e2 lulled us into a false sense of security, and now suddenly the h4 attack.
Very dangerous. The typical response is h5, stopping White's h-pawn.
The knight to e5, in some lines preparing a quick g4.

We have to get this knight off the board ASAP, so the knight to d7 is standard — otherwise White plays g4 and crashes through, and we could get mated. If White plays g4, my plan is the knight takes e5, d takes e5, the knight takes g4 — in time to eliminate the g-pawn while keeping the kingside intact.

Jobava players like to keep the tension with a move like the queen to d2. Once White plays h4, it's clear that in almost every case White castles queenside — so we're heading for an opposite-side-castling position with attacks on both wings. f3 is a very good move, preparing g4; our opponent is showing fantastic knowledge of the system's ideas.
We could play the queen to b6 hitting b2, or the queen to a5, but I'll implement a creative idea — we take on e5, capturing on e5.
White recaptures, capturing on e5. One drawback of f3 is that it weakens e3 — that pawn is now a target.

I'll play the unconventional bishop to h6 — within the framework of attacking the weak e3 pawn it makes sense. Players find it awkward to move the bishop off its fianchetto spot, but here it works, especially because if White pushes e4, he'll struggle to castle queenside, since our bishop will be holding c1. So e4 is way over-ambitious.
If White plays the queen to d2 — the standard defence of the pawn — then our bishop exerts nasty long-term pressure on this diagonal. Now we prepare for White most likely castling queenside next.

If White castles queenside, we'd want a queenside attack — so preemptively, b5 might discourage it. It's like a lead-off in baseball, stepping off the base ready for the pitch. If White doesn't castle queenside, b5 costs nothing and grabs space; if White does, we've gained a tempo, our attack already started. And every tempo is crucial in opposite-side castling, since White will try to get g4 going.

White takes their time with the bishop to d3, a nice move — I assume preparing to meet things with the knight to e2, a high-level idea. Our options: drop the knight back to d7 to trade off that annoying bishop; or something tactical like c5 for pandemonium; or b4, the knight to e2, then c5, staking a big central claim; or the knight to d7, the bishop to f4, the bishop to g7 to prepare e5.
The knight-d7, bishop-f4 trade looks sterile, so let's go crazy — b4, chasing the knight and forcing a decision.
The knight to e2.
And the follow-up, c5.
Why start with b4? First, to expand on the queenside; second, we were threatening c4, which would trap the bishop. White plays c3.
White's treating this like a London. We take, capturing on c3, to fully discourage White from castling queenside.
White recaptures, capturing on c3. We've opened the queenside and prevented queenside castling, which would now be madness with the b-file open — very easy to reach White's king.
Now the second idea — the knight back to d7 — to open the centre. Why? Because White's king is stuck in the middle.
White can castle kingside, but then the h4 pawn becomes a major liability; queenside castling is easy to punish; and if White stays in the centre and we open it, we get to the king.
So we drop the bishop back to its fianchetto square, g7, preparing e5 — which would blast open the centre and open the bishop's diagonal, with very positive consequences.

The rook to d1 — clearly our opponent sees the idea and discourages e5. Do we push anyway? If e5, d takes e5, knight takes e5, there's the weird bishop-e4, and our d5 pawn crumbles a bit — so maybe prepare one more move.
We play the bishop to b7 — which seems silly in isolation, biting on granite, but after e5 and the trade it makes sure the d5 pawn isn't a soft target for White's heavy pieces on the d-file.
g4 — now things really heat up, and I'll likely go quiet as it gets tactical. After take, take on h5, we push e5, feeling good for Black.
We take, capturing on g4 — starting with e5 first would allow g takes h5, which feels scary and could get us mated, so this order first.
White recaptures, capturing on g4. I'm not ruling out getting mated, but with accurate play I hope not.
Now e5, opening the centre and striking at White's well-protected d4 pawn — things really heat up.
The bishop to g3. Time's fine — four minutes, plenty. We force another decision.
We could snap off a pawn, but I go with my gut — the rook to e8, keeping the tension and preparing e takes d4, putting the rook in an x-ray with the king.
White castles kingside, abandoning the mating ambitions for king safety — probably the right call. I underestimated that move.
The knight to f6 — actually the immediate knight to f6 is a smart alternative, with tactics behind it I'll explain after the game.
g5 — most people eye the bishop takes e5. What if White just snaps the pawn? The knight to g4 or the knight to h5 make sense.
Let's go knight to g4, going after the e3 pawn. Maybe the knight to h5 and the queen to d7 was better, but too late now.
The knight to g4 is probably a mistake, but not so bad. White plays the bishop to b5.
We could take on d4, but why not calmly bring the rook up to e7, also solidifying the very valuable f7 pawn?
White takes the pawn, capturing on c5. Now we'd love to win it back.

We can win it back with the queen — the queen to c8 makes most sense, with more tactics behind it: if White pushes c6, after the trade White can't take on d5, because we'd pick up the e3 pawn with a fork. That's why I didn't play the rook to c8.

White pushes c6, we take with the queen, White takes with the bishop, and we recapture, capturing on c6 with the bishop — and once we collect the c5 pawn we'll have an intact centre, excellent coordination with both bishops fianchettoed, and White's pawns terribly weak.
White plays c6 and the bishop to f2 — but we're very close to winning; he wants to take on d5.

Let's solidify — the rook to d8, protecting d5 and bringing the rook into play. I expect e4, then we double on the d-file and blast through the centre. Black is borderline winning, strategically, given how many weaknesses White has.
The knight to g3. If I keep my clock under control, we're going to win.
e4 — not sure it's best, but it opens our bishop and creates strongholds for our knight, which can circle back to e5.
The rook to c1.
The knight to e5 — very juicy squares, and the queen can drive in on the light squares too.
White's starting to crumble. The knight to f3 — an outpost, also hitting the h4 pawn.

We capture, taking on h4 with check — not just for the free pawn, but because now the g5 pawn is a huge weakness.
The king to h3 — and I see a mating net forming around it.

The rook to h1 — I'm not worried about anything on the h-file; there's no attack.

White literally can't move because of this knight.

node.idea: We answer the king's pawn with the knight to f6 — the Alekhine, a rare but sound choice.
White plays e5.
White chases with e5 and our knight hops to d5.
White expands with c4.
We retreat the knight to b6.
White plays d4, taking the centre in a measured way.
We strike back with d6.
White captures on d6 — one of the two main lines.

We recapture with the c-pawn on d6 — my recommendation for Alekhine beginners, because it teaches you to handle an imbalanced structure: White gets a queenside pawn majority, we get a kingside majority.
White develops the knight to c3. Our light-squared bishop will struggle to get out, so we'll fianchetto.
We play g6, preparing the fianchetto.
The bishop settles on g7.

We continue naturally with the knight to c6, and the plan writes itself: press White's two central pawns. It resembles a Dragon but far calmer — both sides castle short and nobody's getting mated soon. It's hard to play at club level for two reasons: you're a touch cramped, so accuracy matters, and you must know how to meet a wide range of White setups.

node.idea: White plays a bishop to c4 — a move, but not the best; we'll cover the theory later.
A knight to b6 — where this knight belongs in the Alekhine — attacking the bishop, so it retreats and loses a tempo.
A bishop to e2 is passive. Our strategy doesn't change: White's e5 pawn is a hook we'll use to contest the center while developing.
The most accurate move is d6, saying we want to remove that e5 pawn — and if we do, White has no central control left.
White plays d4 to fight for the center. Now a knight to c6 makes sense — the way to stop your pieces being trampled by pawns is to combine piece moves with pawn moves, so the pawns act as anchors.
Is d5 a problem before we play the knight to c6? Look carefully — no, because d5 loses control of e5 and drops a pawn.
White plays a knight to f3. Now we transform the position — a bishop to g4 is obvious, but in the spirit of positional chess we take on e5 into an endgame.
We capture on e5.
If White recaptures with the knight, a knight to d4 wins a pawn; he takes with the pawn instead.

We trade queens, and now that e5 pawn becomes a huge weakness — that's the whole point of the Alekhine: White has more central control, but he'll likely lose that pawn or wreck his pieces defending it.
How do we pressure e5? First its defender, the knight — a bishop to g4.

Critical moment: don't just grab on f3 and e5, because it drops the b7 pawn — and even if it didn't, giving up that g4 bishop isn't clearly worth a pawn. The threat is stronger than the execution: keeping him tortured by the weak pawn beats winning it and relieving him.
So we castle long, defending b7, keeping pressure on the bishop and mobilizing our knight. Now we threaten to take on f3, but we could also just keep pressing with e6.
White plays a knight to d2 — a bit of a panic; a knight to g5 would have dropped the bishop to two attackers.
We win a piece — take the bishop, which also pins the rook, rather than traveling to g4.
We take the pawn on e5 — otherwise a knight to a3 could defend.
White plays a knight to c3. Now we just play e6.
e6, to get our bishop out.
White plays a knight to e4, untangling. We could take the rook, but I like just developing — trading on your own terms forces the opponent into uncomfortable decisions.
A bishop to e7 is fine — its main job here is to connect the rooks; it restricts the e4 knight and controls g5. Not every piece has to climb Everest at once.
White plays a bishop to f4, also controlling d8, and attacks our knight — we can move it with tempo.
A knight to g6, in Alekhine spirit — and it sets a trap: a bishop to g3 loses a piece.
White sees it and plays a bishop to e3 — little relief. That e4 knight has been a recurring theme: a central piece still vulnerable to pawns.

The Najdorf's signature move: a6, dear to every Sicilian player. Its first point is simple — it covers b5, keeping White's knight and bishop off that square.

White chooses the bishop to e2 — a very popular reply, and White's quietest. But "quiet" is relative: the position stays sharp. It's called quiet because here White castles short, whereas in the bishop-g5 and bishop-b3 systems White castles long and both sides storm opposite wings.
We play e5. To an outsider this looks bizarre — if it doesn't strike you as strange, you're missing something. ...e6 would give the Scheveningen; the ...e5 Najdorf is our choice.

White retreats the knight to b3. Now, why does ...e5 look like a blunder? It weakens the d6-pawn and, above all, the d5-square. This is exactly why the Najdorf isn't for beginners — you're breaking basic positional rules, and you only earn that right once you truly know them. There's no single reason ...e5 holds up; it's a web of them, and the first is the most basic: we get on with development.

We develop the bishop to e7 — the main move, readying quick castling; the c8-bishop may later fianchetto to b7. Here's the first strand of the web: we have a crowd of pieces to fight for the d5-square.

White castles. Concretely: our bishop can go to e6 and the f6-knight be backed up by its partner from d7 — two pieces directly and one indirectly guarding d5, so White can rarely plant a knight there and make it stick.

We castle. The second strand: we get counterplay on both wings, the ...b5 advance in particular offsetting the d5 weakness. Even so, the hole is real — a knight that lands on d5 and stays can decide the game, so it must be respected, never ignored.
White tries f4. It's playable, but without the bite it would carry if our pawn were back on e6 — here we can simply take on f4.

This capture on f4 followed by the knight to e5 is one of the oldest, most classical Najdorf ideas.

Black develops the knight to c6. We keep developing as though Black exerts no pressure on d4. One common beginner mistake here is the bishop to b5 — not because it drops a piece, since after a queen-a5 check there's the knight to c3, but conceptually: the bishop on b5 is a paper tiger, and Black just blocks with the bishop to d7.

The best square for our bishop is d3, for several reasons. With a pawn on d4 like this, placing the bishop behind it is good practice: if Black castles kingside — the likeliest direction — we'll have a Greek-gift sacrifice ready.

Black's queenside pawns look imposing, and b5 is actually a good move — but Black has bitten off more than she can chew, pushing all those pawns without piece support. We'll use OUR pawns, a very typical idea, to break down the whole chain.

node.idea: We open e4 and meet a French — e6, preparing to challenge our center with d5.
d4, grabbing the full center. This is the heart of the French: our broad pawn duo against Black's coming counterstrike.

d5, and we're at an early crossroads. In earlier speedruns I've recommended the Nimzowitsch Advance — e5, and after c5 you skip the automatic c3 and develop the knight instead, voluntarily giving up the pawn chain and inviting a capture on d4. It's counterintuitive, with a deep positional underpinning, and genuinely dangerous for an unprepared opponent.
But today I'll play the line I'm most comfortable with, the one I've played my whole life — the Tarrasch, the knight to d2.
The knight to d2 is what defines the Tarrasch. It shields e4 without blocking the c-pawn, keeping c3 in reserve to buttress d4.
A quick primer if you don't know the French: against d5 White's most natural, most popular try is a knight to c3.
But a knight to c3 leads to incredibly theoretical waters we don't want to touch with a ten-foot pole, and the Exchange is equally to be avoided. The Tarrasch is the answer.
The Tarrasch straddles the bridge — it isn't drowning in theory, yet it carries real venom that lets you crush an unprepared opponent. Against it Black has two main replies.
e5 gains space and shoves the f6 knight back, locking the center into that Advanced-French shape.
The knight retreats to d7, ready to regroup and to help hit our chain with a later c5 or f6.
The main line is the bishop to d3 — the most natural square, and one that already eyes the h7 pawn for a future kingside strike.
Black plays c5, striking at the base of our chain, the d4 pawn.
And here we do play c3. Don't file this under the Advance variation — this pawn structure shows up across many French lines, and the Advance has very different piece configurations for both sides.
Black develops the knight to c6, and there's actually very little in common between this Tarrasch line and a true Advanced French.
Because breaking up your own pawn chain like that is strategically undesirable.

You can end up losing the e5 pawn with little compensation. There's a line with a queen to e2, the only way to hold both pawns, but after the queen drops to c7 it's already very hard for White to defend.
If White plays h3, that often makes it worse, because g4 comes and can rip open the h-file — the last thing you want.
After h5 the g4 break looms and the h-file opens.

That opponent was the Indian grandmaster Abhijeet Gupta, and after the game I went back to the drawing board — I got smashed.
The refutation involved a capture on g4 that tore my kingside apart, and only afterward did I build a genuinely good system against g5.

We develop the bishop to c4 — this is the Scotch Gambit, a hybrid of the Scotch and the Italian. It's a genuinely dangerous, grandmaster-approved weapon, and a fine alternative if you like the Evans Gambit; at club level its traps bring quick wins.

Black plays d6, a solid, slightly passive choice that sidesteps the gambit's traps — a line playable with the black pieces too, leaving a marginally worse game. The point of the early bishop, as in the Italian, is access to the g5-square, where a knight or bishop is a key resource in many lines.

We recapture on d4 with the knight, regaining the gambit pawn and opening lines. White has the pleasant side — better central control, the bishop raking from c4 as in a good Scotch, and the sacrificed pawn already back.
Black develops the knight to f6. Should we fear a capture on d4 that drops the queen into the centre?

We develop the knight to c3. No — a capture on d4 wouldn't scare us: Black has no second knight on b8 to come to c6 and harass the queen, so it would just be well-placed for us to strike at. This is the same solid setup you can reach through a Philidor move order.

The move that permanently removes that idea is the bishop to b3: it drops the bishop onto a defended square, out of reach of a future ...d5 pawn fork.

Black plays the bishop to g4, hitting the queen — but that's all it does, and the bishop can land in real trouble. Where to put the queen? On a square where it also does something: d2 is awkward and d3 is covered by the knight, so the queen goes to e1 — from there it can later swing to g3, and it doesn't block our bishop. Simple logic is often the right logic.
The queen steps to e1, eyeing the later lift to g3 to x-ray the king.

We play Bologan's move, b6 — sidestepping theory. It heads for a fianchetto without the drawback of ...d6: if White takes on c6 we keep the queen recapture that supports our c5-bishop, and that bishop is now anchored by the b6-pawn.

White plays f4, the main move — but it threatens little. If you fear e5: with our bishop soon on b7, that push has a real cost, opening the long diagonal for the bishop, and our queen could swing to g6 hitting g2. There's the awkward f5 in reply, so it may be wiser to route the queen to h6, where White can't play f5 because his e3-bishop would hang.
We develop straightforwardly with the bishop to b7. It looks scary opposite White's centre, but just developing pieces can't be that bad.
White pushes e5. It looks menacing, but there's nothing to attack — you can't be blown off the board without targets and weaknesses, and we have none.

We play the queen to h6, as planned. White's pawns look intimidating but they're stuck in molasses — and the queen sets a hidden threat: an x-ray works both ways, so our queen now x-rays the undefended bishop on e3, making ...Nxe5 a real threat. A further cost of f4: any capture on e3 now comes with check.

node.idea: White opens with the pawn to d4, and we answer the knight to f6. It's been ages since we faced d4 — and this becomes a Trompowsky.
The bishop to g5 — the Trompowsky, one of the non-c4 sidelines. The London system has largely eclipsed it in popularity these days.

The standard reply is the knight to e4, challenging the bishop at once. Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Gambit players might prefer the pawn to e6, but the knight jump is the principled try and worth learning.
White plays the bishop to f4 — the main response, keeping the bishop and stepping out of the knight's way.
White has three real tries here: the aggressive pawn to h4 sideline popularized by English players like Hodgson, the retreat to e3, and the main bishop to f4.

So the knight comes back to f6 — no reason to leave it on e4: letting White take there would ruin our structure, hand White a target and extra central control. There's nothing lost: both sides have spent a tempo, the knight to e4 and back, the bishop to g5 and to f4 — it balances.
White develops the knight to f3.

So we play the pawn to e6 and carry on as if nothing's happening — the bishops aren't bothering us. If White ever takes our bishop, we recapture with the h-pawn and our rook is developed for free; we just keep the tension in mind and stay alert for the moment taking on d3 becomes right.
White jumps the knight to e5. Now we orchestrate our own version of the standoff, with the bishop to d6.
The bishop to d6 makes a lot of sense — developing and asking White the very same question White asked us.

If White captures on f6, then the bishop takes the queen, White takes on g7, and we play the rook to g8 — White gets at most two pieces for the queen. By inducing the pawn to f3, we've weakened White's king, and now the knight can drop back to d7.

node.idea: At a lower level, h4 — the Hodgson variation, a very double-edged move — causes consternation. Its idea is simple: it defends the bishop, and if Black takes on g5, White recaptures with the h-pawn, opening the h-file (Black has the h7 pawn, restricting the rook) and creating a deep-freeze — the g5 pawn making it very hard for Black to ever fix the h7 weakness, since after h6 White takes and damages Black's kingside. So taking the bishop isn't best.

Black has many options; I'll play it simply with d5 — occupy the centre and toss the ball back. h4's drawback, beyond not developing, is that it commits White to an uncertain king: kingside castling is unlikely with the damage, queenside is risky with the knight on e4, and staying central is dubious.

The knight to d2 — he knows his theory. I don't want to take on g5, which plays into White's hands; instead I'll simply drop the knight back to f6 or d6, a symmetrical Queen's-Gambit-Declined-type position.
The knight back to f6. Moving the same piece three times seems wrong, but the centre is closed, so the effect is diminished — and White spent tempi on the weakening h4.

e3. The point of the knight's to-and-fro: we induced h4, provoking a serious kingside weakness, and now develop conventionally. We've been move-ordered into a reverse Queen's Gambit Declined — where White plays c4, we play c5 from the black side, but after c5 we must watch d takes c5.
Since White is developed, after c5, d takes c5, e6, White solidifies with b4 — so we start with the solid e6 and follow with c5 to contest and pressure White's centre.

The knight to e2. Let's play c5 — we can also throw in h6 to force the bishop to commit, but no rush; this pin isn't dangerous, since an easy test is whether the pinned piece is protected by a pawn, and it is.
We play c5, and White takes, capturing on c5.
We recapture with the bishop, capturing on c5 — precisely why we started with e6.
White's knights on e2 and d2 are passive; a3 is a good move, preparing b4. Many would auto-play a5, but not every idea must be prevented — b4 isn't a threat, just an idea; what does b4 actually do?

b4 chases our bishop from c5 — but the bishop is happy to drop to e7, ending the pin. So we develop the knight to c6. And after b4, that pawn becomes a target: we chisel with a5 once White's pawn is on b4 — the base of the chain, or sometimes the tip.
The knight to f4 — a perfect chance for the move I mentioned earlier: the bishop on g5 is now fully deprived of squares.
So it's time for h6, forcing White to trade the bishop for the knight, capturing on f6, letting our queen come to the active f6.
We recapture with the queen, capturing on f6. White has traded the dark-squared bishop, the pride of the Trompowsky — a great position for us.

The queen on f6 attacks b2 and pressures f2 — Black's already better. The knight to h5. We can grab the pawn on b2: people fear the queen getting trapped, but calculate concretely — after the queen takes b2, the rook to b1, our queen defends g7, so we drop it to e5, not c3 where the rook to b3 chases it; the central queen looks vulnerable to f4, but f4 gives up e3 with check.

The queen takes, capturing on b2. After the rook to b1, the queen to e5 — and if White chases with the knight, it severs the connection to the h5-knight, letting us take on h5. So we can safely take b2. Even if e5 were unavailable, taking on a3 would be fine — a king move to f8 isn't the end of the world.
The bishop to e2. We have ways to deal with g7 — g6 is the forcing option, or we simply castle. The king is safest on f8, surrounded by pawn cover; d7 walks into the d-file x-ray.

Castling kills two birds — it develops and protects g7. If I were White I'd contemplate g4 for kingside counterplay, using the uncastled king: the trope where the uncastled side can benefit from the h1-rook if the h-file opens — see Vukovic's Art of Attack.

Now up two pawns — remember diminishing returns: the second pawn matters more than the third. White plays e4, a great-looking move that does nothing: d5 is defended by the e6 pawn, and if White takes on d5 and we recapture, our light bishop opens up — we'd welcome White taking on e4. Not the knight to b4 or d4 grabbing c2 — that's greed too far, our pieces clustering on the queenside with the queen overextended after the rook to b1. Instead, improve: our a3-bishop is awkward and ties the queen down, so move it.
The bishop to b4 pins the d2-knight, but that pin is temporary — White castles and the bishop looks silly. I like the bishop to d6, where the pressure is meaningful.

The rook to b1 chases the queen from b2 — glad we moved the bishop off a3. Where to? Not the queen to c3, chased by the rook to b3; I like the queen to f6, though it runs into the knight to h5, then the queen to e7.
Or the queen to d4 — I like that most, because it's very hard to attack: if the d2-knight moves, it opens a queen trade.

tree.outro: That's the heart of the Four Knights Game, Scotch Variation.

node.idea: We take the white pieces and open with the king's pawn; Black answers symmetrically with e5, a reply we haven't met in a while. Into it we've been alternating two systems — the Vienna and the Four Knights Scotch — and today we steer for the Scotch.
The king's knight develops to f3, the first step into the Four Knights.
Black brings a knight to c6, and we mirror with the queen's knight to c3. Both sides simply develop the knights first; once Black adds the knight to f6, we're set to break in the centre.
Black plays the last knight to f6, and now the point of the system: d4, striking the e5-pawn with every piece already developed.

Instead of resolving the centre, Black steps the bishop to b4 — a rare sideline here that we've almost never faced, and a touch passive. The main road would have been the capture on d4, we retake with the knight, and only then the bishop to b4. This is playable, but it leaves White a small edge.

We must not grab with the pawn: after taking on e5 the knight springs to e4 and hits our c3-knight. Instead we push d5, seizing space and locking the centre. Black sometimes steers into this very structure with the black pieces, because it forces White to close up and gives the second player something to play for — though positionally Black is simply more cramped.
Black swings the knight from c6 to e7, heading for g6.

We develop the bishop to d3, defending e4 and drawing the sting from any jump to e4 — with that square covered, the knight can no longer hit our c3-knight with tempo. And we're untroubled by a capture on c3.
Black bolsters the centre with d6. We're not afraid of the trade on c3: yes, it damages our pawns, but in return we get the bishop pair and the chance to buttress the centre with c4.
We castle kingside. We could also slip in h3 to discourage the bishop coming to g4, but that pin is toothless here — Black's pieces are too passive to make anything of it.
Black captures on c3. Had he tried the bishop to g4 instead, we'd have answered h3 to chase it back, and could even have followed with g4.
We recapture with the b-pawn, accepting the doubled c-pawns in exchange for the bishop pair and a broad centre.

Black lands the knight on g6 — the correct setup in this closed centre. And that's the lesson of these positions: when the centre is locked, the worth of any single move drops. Move orders turn flexible; what matters is reaching the right setup and the right plan, not the exact sequence.
We begin with h3, denying the bishop the g4-square. In a closed position the emphasis shifts from the individual move to the overall aim.
Black castles. Another strong move for us is c4, reinforcing the d5-pawn.
We play c4, cementing d5 and hinting at a future c5 break.
Black plays b6, holding the queenside confidently. We simply keep developing.

The bishop to g5 would catch the eye, but Black just plays h6 and shoos it away — so we settle for the bishop to e3, completing our development. Now we can turn to the side where we hold the edge: the kingside. On the queenside we'll never get in c5; on the kingside we have more force gathered.
Black centralizes the queen to e7. Our development is done, and the extra pieces sit on the kingside — that's where the game will be decided, and we have several promising ideas there.
We tuck the king to h2 — a quiet move with a double purpose that will show itself: it is at once prophylactic and aggressive.
Black lunges the knight to h5, aiming for f4. Now the point of the king move surfaces: it is prophylaxis against exactly this, and our reply is g3.

We meet it with g3. This is only safe because the king stands on h2 — otherwise the h3-pawn could fall to a sacrifice; with the king there, that door is shut. And why did Black go to h5 at all? He is angling for f5, but it fails tactically: after f5 we take, the bishop retakes, we take again, the rook recaptures, and g4 at the very end forks the rook and the knight. There is a hidden cost to the knight sitting on h5 too — our queen x-rays it straight through our own f3-knight, so we can lift that knight, which we wanted to do anyway to prepare f4, and chase the h5-knight back to f6, gaining a tempo on our own plan.

Black retreats the knight to f6. With the knight back, we press on — but carefully. Play the knight to d2 now and the queen comes to d7, forcing g4; and g4 fatally weakens the f4-square, killing the very break we're preparing.
So we play the knight back to g1, preemptively: it guards h3 and clears the path to prepare f4. We're not ready to play f4 just yet.

Black plays the knight to d7 — pre-moved, so he never saw the queen-to-d7 resource. But committing to a plan doesn't mean closing your eyes: you must read how the opponent's move reshapes the position. And f4 still carries a serious flaw — after f4, the capture on f4, and g-takes-f4, Black strikes back with f5, and once the centre opens our e3-bishop falls under the queen's x-ray, so taking on f5 walks into tactics that leave our king badly exposed. Piling another defender on f4 with the knight to e2 isn't the cure; the cure is to shield the bishop first — but there's no time, because after the queen to d2 the knight swings to c5 and the break fails anyway, since capturing on f4 leaves our e4-pawn hanging.

So we change tack — shelve f4 for now and open a second front with h4. It doesn't come from nowhere: the g3-pawn supports the advance. Worried about the sacrifice on h4? The knight takes, g-takes, queen-takes-h4 with check, and we simply slide the king to g2 — and here the knight on g1 earns its keep, guarding h3, so once Black's d7-knight moves there's no check on h3. The upside of h4: the straightforward h5 next, shoving the g6-knight to the rim; the knight on g1 is freed and the h3-pawn stops being a worry — the queen can still reach h3, but no longer with a capture — and we may win the g5-square as an outpost for the bishop.

Black jumps the knight to c5. A healthy positional move for us either way — and we haven't wholly abandoned f4, though with the pawn heading to h5 it's far less likely: once h5 is in, an f4 break would only gut our own king, so we'd allow it only under perfect circumstances. Black is playing this very well.
We push h5. This can hardly hurt — and it looks like the knight is more or less forced to h8, buried on the edge.

Instead Black finds the knight to f4 — I'll admit I missed it. Does it work? The lines run deep: it holds tactically to a draw by perpetual, but it doesn't win. And crucially we don't have to take it — we can capture on c5 first, which may be the real solution.
We take on c5 first with the bishop. Now the queen to h4 is not mate, because the g3-pawn covers that square.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn on c5. There was a very specific reason to take on c5 first.
Now g-takes-f4 works — though it's razor-thin, move-for-move calculation where you get it exactly right or lose ground.
Black checks with the queen on h4.

We step the king to g2. The looming idea is the queen to f3 — a genuinely frightening move; there may be a hidden win for Black I can't see, but move-for-move I believe we hold. Behind these choices sit the details: if the bishop comes to g4 now, we take on e5, and the bishop to h3 only looks like it traps the queen — our knight swings in, takes the bishop and defends the queen at once; and if Black tries a perpetual with the queen to g5 and back to h4, that same knight blocks on h3.

tree.outro: That's the heart of the Grünfeld Defense (Brinckmann Attack).

node.idea: White plays d4, and we develop the knight to f6, keeping our options open.
White grabs space with c4, and we fianchetto with g6 — heading for a Grünfeld this time rather than the King's Indian.
The knight to c3. The Grünfeld, unlike the King's Indian, meets this with d5, not d6.

We strike in the centre with d5 — the Grünfeld, universally regarded as one of the best objective defenses to d4. Nobody has found an advantage against it anywhere; the downside is just the out-of-this-world amount of theory to play it professionally.
The bishop to f4 is a legitimate try. The Grünfeld's idea is simple: we grab central control by combining the King's Indian fianchetto with a proactive d5, instead of letting White build with e4.
We don't take the c4 pawn — that's not the point. The point is rapid development so we can attack White's centre; it's a hypermodern opening. So the bishop goes to g7, and c6 is unnecessary.
We're perfectly happy to recapture on d5 with the knight. White takes, capturing on d5.
The knight takes, capturing on d5.

The bishop to g3 is correct. What makes the Grünfeld both fun and hard is constant tactical alertness — these centralized pieces are integral to Black's central strategy, and unlike the King's Indian, where you play the long game, here you assault White's centre directly, with moves like c5 and the knight to c6. White can lose quickly if he doesn't develop precisely. So between c5 and the knight to c6, which harasses the centre more effectively?

It's c5 — the knight to c6 can be met by e3, forming a pawn chain, but c5 is very strong: if White simply takes with d takes c5, we play the knight takes c3, and after trading queens he loses a piece, because he can't recapture the bishop takes c3 with check between the king and rook. If instead e3, after the trade he gets an isolated queen pawn and we blockade the square in front of it — phenomenal for Black.

node.idea: We meet the king's pawn with c6 — the Caro-Kann.

Here's the whole reason the Caro exists: unlike the French, we get to develop this light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain, to f5, before we ever shut it in with e6 — and that's exactly what we've done. White answers with f4, grabbing more central space, but it's not a good move: it curbs the development of White's own light bishop and it weakens his king.
The proper reply is e6 — White has over-committed his pawns while lagging in development.

White develops the bishop to d3. Since this is our first Advance Caro, here's the rationale. The centre is CLOSED, and a closed centre is built of pawn chains — our black pawns form one chain, and d4 with e5 is White's chain. The side with more levers, more ability to attack and undermine the OTHER side's chain, is the side holding the initiative — and the whole point of the Caro is that Black is that side. White's compensation is space; those two things balance out. And right now we don't want to surrender this prime parking spot on f5 so easily — we trade it on OUR terms.
Trading on our own terms means: when this bishop comes off, we want to replace it with a KNIGHT. So the typical move is the knight to h6 — and if White takes on f5, we recapture with the knight.
White develops the knight to f3. Why do we want our knight to reach f5? To pressure d4. So the question becomes how we keep piling onto that pawn.
We play c5 — hitting the base of White's pawn chain, and at the same time opening the c6 square for our knight.

White castles. Now we could grab d4 at once, but to play it cleanly there's a subtlety worth a second — and note White can also take on c5, which we'll deal with.

Rather than snatch d4 immediately, we play the knight to c6 first — the more flexible move, since we want it on the board regardless. The queen to b6 is also possible, but we hold it in reserve: if White plays c3, THEN the queen to b6 becomes strong.
White plays c3, showing his intent to prop up d4.

Now the clean way is to take on d4 first and then play the queen to b6, winning the pawn — and in a real game that's what I'd do. But I want to show a beautiful idea, so I play the queen to b6 first, hoping he grabs a pawn.

White finds g4. Here's a common trap — tunnel vision. After a move like the bishop to d4, many players automatically snatch the rook on a1. But look wider: taking on a1 gives up our knight, so White gets a knight back for the rook — a real chunk of material. So we do NOT grab the rook immediately.

Black plays the knight to c6, and here a rule worth remembering: an idea that failed in one position can suddenly work in another — now d5 is strong, a tempo push on the knight that also denies Black the time for the blockading ...Bd6. Prevent ...Bd6 with the bishop to f4, since that bishop is Black's only way to blockade the passed pawn — kept out, the passer becomes a huge asset. A few threads run through the finish: when you're a pawn up, unlike a piece up, you generally do NOT want to trade queens, as it relieves the defender; the g5-pin is dangerous, all the more with the queen already eyeing the knight; and combinations are built by stacking threats — a capture on f6 opens the g-file for a queen check on g3, while a rook to d1 x-rays the queen, so a discovered check wins material. Principled development plus these small, flexible observations is what makes strong players win almost automatically.

The knight to c3 — flexible: let's see how Black develops before deciding, because if the knight comes to f6, the pawn to f4 gets much stronger.

Black plays the bishop to b4 — good. We're not scared of the capture on c3: we'll castle kingside and don't mind the doubled pawns. And notice both the bishop and the e5-knight are undefended — which points to the queen to d4.
The queen to d4, hitting both loose pieces. The knight to c6 blunders g7, the bishop retreat or the capture on c3 are big wins for us — the only save is the queen to e7.

Black finds the queen to e7. That's usually why the queen to d4 is dubious — but here there's an extenuating factor: the g7-pawn is vulnerable, the c3-knight is pinned, and we can chase the e5-knight with f4.

Black plays the knight to g6 — the point: after the knight to c6 and the capture on g7, the rook hangs, but on g6 the knight defends the rook. The capture on g7 also allows the nasty reply of the queen taking e4.
We take on g7 with check anyway — we can't take the queen because of the pin, and c2 hangs, so it's a mess, but there's an interesting idea I just spotted.

The king to d1 — the exception to not moving the king early. Blocking with the knight buries the bishop, and c2 would hang with a cascade of problems. Instead the king to d1 opens our attack on the queen and, crucially, the e-file — it's a race to land a rook there, and Black can't castle short with our queen on g7.

We take on g7 with check anyway — we can't take the queen because of the pin, and c2 hangs, so it's a mess, but there's an interesting…
Black plays the knight to g6 — the point: after the knight to c6 and the capture on g7, the rook hangs, but on g6 the knight defends…
The pawn to f4.
Black finds the queen to e7.
The queen to d4, hitting both loose pieces.
Black plays the bishop to b4 — good.
The knight to c3 — flexible: let's see how Black develops before deciding, because if the knight comes to f6, the pawn to f4 gets much stronger.
Black recaptures with the knight on e5.
We capture on e5.
Black plays the knight to c6, declining the gambit — it transposes to a Nimzowitsch setup, and it's not a bad move.

node.idea: We open e4, and our opponent plays the Sicilian, c5.
The Alapin move, c3.
We face d5, the direct counter in the centre.
We take, capturing on d5.
The queen recaptures on d5, and we play d4 — a highly theoretical position we've had many times.
The knight to f6, the main move.
We develop our own knight to f3 — all theory. Black is at a major crossroads with four or so worthy options.

The knight to c6 — the natural move if you're seeing this for the first time. Its drawback: the f8-bishop stays locked behind the e7 pawn. The course's best way to punish it exploits exactly that: after d takes c5, Black can't recapture on c5 with the bishop, so the queen must take, handing White tempi. So the move is d takes c5.
We take, capturing on c5 — you might be reluctant, since it lets Black trade queens and drive our king out for a pawn, and you might think c5 is easy to win back, but that's far from true.
The queen takes d1 with check, and our king recaptures on d1 — if he knows the theory, this gets sharp.

a5, a very understandable move preventing b4 — but that doesn't mean we must part with the c5 pawn. We have many ways to cling to it, though not at the cost of our position. The bishop to e3 runs into the knight to g4, ruining our structure; h3 to meet e6 with the bishop to e3 runs into the knight to d5; and a3 with b4 fails to a takes b4, c takes b4, the knight takes b4. So a more indirect approach — a5 weakens the b5 square.

The bishop to b5 has limited value since Black plays e6, so I like the Alapin-esque idea of getting the knight to b5. So the knight to a3 — from b5 the knight eyes c7, and if Black pushes the e-pawn and we play the knight to b5, we can even reach d6, where after Black takes and we recapture, we get the bishop pair and dark-square control; even if Black wins the pawn back, we'd get the better endgame. A nice flexible developing move, waiting for Black to show his cards.

It may seem like one-move-itis, but it's a serious threat: to stop the knight to c7, Black must ruin his king safety by moving the king to the d-file, or lose queenside castling by moving the rook — either way a wasted move. The king to d8.

Now our knight on b5 just chills. We could also go from the other side with the knight to g5 — sticking knights on b5 and g5, hitting f7 and c7. Black would play g6 to defend f7, and after f4 Black could counter with h6. Or the straightforward bishop to c4, simple and strong. The knight to g5 is the move to win on the spot — I'm going for the throat, and it's not a big commitment: knights move backwards.

The bishop to e6 immediately justifies the knight to g5, because we have the standing option of taking on e6 and permanently wrecking Black's structure — I'll take those doubled pawns any day. You don't have to take immediately, but not having to rush a move doesn't mean you shouldn't play it.

I don't see a reason to keep the knight there, so let's take on e6 while we can. Now the e6 pawn is one of Black's main weaknesses — we could hit it with a rook to e1, but I see a more effective, unconventional development: getting the bishop to h3 or g4, either via the bishop to e2 and g4, or g3 and the bishop to h3, which I call the hyper-fianchetto.
I like g3 — it's a bit more elegant.
We follow up with our plan, the bishop to h3.

e5 — its obvious drawback is that the d5-knight loses its support. The idea plays itself: we want a rook on d1, not to attack the knight in some random way; if the bishop to b6, the knight drops to c7 and we've achieved nothing.

So instead we move the king off d1 — to the c-file or e-file, doesn't matter; I like keeping the king central in the endgame. The king to e2. Notice how our pawns restrict both black knights — d4, b4 and f4 are all covered, a major appeal of g3 over the bishop-e2 route. Now the devastating threat of the rook to d1, and Black is borderline dead lost — not just from the extra pawn, but because his position is in shambles. He can't castle, the king has moved; against the rook to d1 there's no good answer — if the king to e8, the rook to d1, and if the rook to d8 defends the knight, we play the rook takes d5, the classic trick with the knight coming to c7 to win the rook. e6 might be the only move for breathing room, but then we take on e6 and Black can resign. What's wrong with the knight to f6? A check on d1 forces the king to e8 — which is partly why we put the bishop on h3: not just to hit e6, but so that when Black played e5 we also contained the king, preventing it from reaching c8.

tree.intro: Let's walk through the Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Declined (Alapin). Watch the ideas as the moves play out.

node.idea: We answer e4 with c5 — the Sicilian, our fighting reply.
d4 already. This is an anti-Sicilian move — the entry point into the Smith-Morra Gambit, where White throws a pawn at us to rip the position open.
We take, capturing on d4. Now White has a choice — recapture, or slip into an open Sicilian with a knight to f3.
c3 — the true Morra pawn offer. Here there's almost an ideological choice: grab the pawn and play right into a Morra player's dream, or refuse it and take the fun out of White's whole setup.
The knight to f6 is that refusal. We won't touch the c3 pawn — that's exactly what Morra specialists want. Instead we hit e4 and steer the game somewhere White is far less prepared for.
e5 lunges forward, kicking our knight. This is the transposition we were after — the pawn structure is now an Alapin, not a gambit.

The knight settles on d5, and we've reached an Alapin Sicilian by force. This is the whole point: instead of memorizing forcing Morra theory where one slip loses in five moves, we've reached a much safer, more understandable structure.

White recaptures on d4, rebuilding the center. The beauty of this whole line is that you can play it without fear — you don't have to know it to the same razor's-edge depth the accepted Morra demands.
d6 immediately, chipping away at White's advanced center. We start questioning that e5 spearhead right away rather than letting White sit comfortably.
A knight to f3 develops and props up e5. Now we have several tries — we could grab on e5 — but the cleanest is the main road.

The knight to c6 is the main, principled continuation, piling on d4 and finishing our development. Against the standard bishop to c4 there's a rare line — one Sam Shankland showed me — that really tests how deep our opponent's theory runs.
But White plays the bishop to d3 instead of c4. The pause before it tells us they're already out of book — this is just a developing move, nothing special, and crucially it doesn't do what c4 would.

So we develop the bishop to g4, eyeing the f3 knight. If White does bail out by capturing on d6, we recapture with the queen and land an ideal isolated-queen's-pawn setup, with our knight already planted on the blockading square in front of that pawn.

White does go queen to b3, we chop on f3, White recaptures with the g-pawn, and we commit to e6. Now the sharp line is queen takes b7, knight takes d4, and the check on b5 has to be reckoned with — we capture the bishop, White checks with the queen from b5, and the point I'd missed at first is that we don't have to run the king to e7; we simply block with the queen to d7, and the resulting endgame favors us because White's pawn structure is a wreck. In the game White actually declines the b7 pawn, which makes our path obvious — keep striking at the center with a capture on e5 while White still can't finish developing. The safe alternatives, a rook to b8 or the queen to d7, were both excellent; honestly the queen to d7 would have been far easier to handle. But we're playing maximally principled, trusting the complications, because our lead in development is enormous and White's whole position is on the verge of collapse.

Our knight is hanging and can't move — a retreat walks into a bishop check on b5 that's mating, and the knight on c6 will be under crushing fire. So the near-automatic move is the bishop check on b4, played essentially without further calculation, because it can only help us: it opens the door to castle kingside — a safety valve, a worst-case escape. Even in the grimmest scenario we could sacrifice the knight on c6, throw a rook to c8 with tempo, and dream of infiltrating on c1 after a knight takes c3. That's all brainstorming, not forced yet.

White blocks with the bishop to d2. The first question I ask is simply: can we castle? If yes, most of our problems dissolve and we never have to shuffle the king to f8. And there's a gorgeous resource lurking — after we castle and White grabs on c6, a rook to c8 sets up a rook lift to c1 with check that isn't a blunder, because the blocking bishop on d2 is pinned. When the king steps to e2 we scoop the rook on h1, and even if White interposes by capturing our bishop, we have one more blow: the knight swings to f4 with a nasty check and then collects the d-pawn with the queen. It all works because White's queenside has never developed.

So we castle — the answer was yes. This is why we did the hard thinking in the opening's first ten moves: now the play is straightforward, and White is simply lost if the calculation holds. Once a queen takes c6 fails to that rook lift, White's position caves in; his queen goes from greatest asset to greatest liability — stranded offside on the queenside, unable to rejoin the game or defend the loose points scattered across the board. White can't even castle safely: a capture on d2 with a queen check on g5 rakes in the minor pieces, and our knight leaping to f4 hits g2 with mate ideas.

White tries a rook to g1. Now we shift from sharp tactics to simple technique. Our knight isn't really hanging — we can leave it on c6 — but why would we, when it has a dream square on d4? After the knight lands on d4 we've checked the ideas: if White captures our bishop, we recapture, and should the queen take on b4 our knight jumps to f3 forking the king and rook while unmasking a discovered hit on the d3 bishop. White can't hold everything together.

We take on d4, and there's nothing to fear — a bishop lunge to h6 at g7 is simply illegal, and there are no pieces near our king for White to attack. The one thing to avoid is pushing the f-pawn, which would allow a lateral back-rank mate. White's best try to stave off the doom is a bishop to e4, since it guards the sore f3 pawn; there's no easy way to hold f3 otherwise. Meanwhile we can pile up on the queenside with a rook to b8 or even set about trapping that stranded queen with a quiet a5.
White does defend with the bishop to e4. Now we just maximize — and the straightforward path is a rook to b8, bringing our last piece into the attack with tempo against the offside queen.

The rook swings to b8. From here it's take the bishop, take the b2 pawn, and our rook roars into the attack while White's queen is hopelessly stranded on a7 — it did its job snatching b7 and a7, but now it can't get home. When you sense the win is close, don't hunt only for mate: look for the move that wins material outright. A knight to c3 is the cleanest, hitting the rook and preparing tactics down the file. There are a dozen winning tries — a queen to h4, a knight to f4 — but the discipline is to choose simple, healthy moves and never blow it chasing a brilliancy: a flashy queen check that lets the king slip out can hand back the whole advantage. White is completely cooked and resigns.

node.idea: We take White and open e4; Black replies e6 — the French. This is our opening-focused run: play principled moves and punish typical non-theoretical setups.
We build the big centre with d4.
Black plays the offbeat ...Nc6 rather than the main ...d5. Don't assume a non-theoretical move means you're already winning; just develop soundly.
We simply develop the knight to f3 — an immediate ...d5 is too concrete before we've developed.
Black plays the passive ...d6. We have several ways to punish it; the simplest is the knight to c3, keeping to the spirit of e4 openings rather than grabbing space with c4.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black develops the knight to f6.

The bishop comes to d3 — it props up e4, and once Black castles short we can push e5 and aim the bishop at h7. Combined with the queen coming to e4, that battery threatens mate on h7. Note: even if Black plays ...h6, the square itself stays weak — don't confuse a weak pawn with a weak square.

Black plays ...h6 and we castle. We're unbothered by ...Nb4 — the bishop just steps back and a3 chases it. Black's slow queenside play neglects his kingside, which we punish by opening the centre: Black's d6- and e6-pawns are hooks, and a pawn advance can act like dynamite to blow the centre open.

Black plays ...b6, and we strike with d5 — the thematic dynamiting of the centre, and crucially it opens the e-file straight at Black's king. If Black takes, we have two defenders to his two attackers; we'd play it even as a sacrifice, because that file is the highway to the king — which is exactly why we castled early.
Black captures on d5.
We recapture with the pawn — a major step toward winning.

Black plays ...Nb4. Our objective now is to keep Black's king stuck in the centre — a moving target is hard to hit. We can't stop ...Be7, but a rook to e1 with check pins it, and by piling pressure on the pinned bishop we keep the king glued to the centre as a defender.
First we insert the check on b5 — avoiding a trade and keeping our light-squared bishop, which rakes the light squares that ...b6 weakened.
Black blocks with the bishop to d7.
We take on d7 with check.

Black recaptures with the queen — the best move, though few under 2000 find it. Beyond the open e-file, I'd spotted that the knight on b4 is horribly exposed: a minor piece parked on the opponent's side is easy prey for pawns.
So we shove it away with a3 — a move you'd want regardless; the knight has to retreat to a6, since capturing just loses it.
The knight lands on a6, loose. Remember the acronym: loose pieces drop off — an undefended piece plus a wide-open king is a fork waiting to happen.
And there it is: the queen to e2 with check forks king and knight — we forget the e-file and simply win the knight on a6, a full piece up.

node.idea: We open e4, and face the Sicilian.
We play the Alapin, c3.

The knight to c6 is one of the most common responses, but it's already a serious inaccuracy — not quite a mistake if Black follows up correctly, but one more slip and things get disastrously bad within five or six moves.
Our response is obvious: c3 prepared d4, and the knight to c6 doesn't stop it — we have enough defenders — so we grab the centre with d4.
Black takes, capturing on d4. The knight to c6 is misplaced here for a simple reason.

We recapture with a pawn, capturing on d4, threatening to push to d5 — and without a pawn shell to support them, Black's pieces get tossed around with no central footholds and can even be trapped. After d5 and the knight to e5, f4 sends the knight all the way back to g6, and the knight to f6 is even worse: after d5, the knight to e5, f4, the knight to g6, e5, the knight has only g8, since g4 and h5 are covered by our queen. A justified violation of opening principles — moving only pawns, but with tempo.

So we either push our own pawn to d5, grabbing the centre and chasing the knight, or just develop with the knight to c3 and the knight to f3. Black plays d5 — and the instinct is to meet it with e5, but that's inaccurate: unlike the Advance French, where Black's pawn is already on e6 giving the bad French bishop, here Black gets a good French or Caro-Kann, bringing the bishop out to f5 first and only then locking with e6.
So we take, capturing on d5, rather than allow that improved French.
