node.idea: We have White and open the pawn to e4, met by e6 — the French Defence.
We play the pawn to e5 — the Steinitz Variation — and I'm a big fan of following up with the knight to f3.
The knight to f3. Black pre-moves the bishop to d7 expecting the pawn to c3 — but we're not going to play c3.
The traditional bishop to d3. The whole point of the Steinitz is that we leave the pawn on d4 and never play c3, conserving that tempo.
We castle — making all the normal French moves except c3.
Black captures on d4. The entire system revolves around the e5-pawn — we over-protect it with everything we have, and recover d4 later by rerouting the knight from d2 to b3.
But first the bishop to f4 to over-protect e5, so we needn't worry about it. Against the queen to b6, don't play b3 — we want that square for our knight — and don't reflexively defend b2 either.

The knight to d2, without defending b2. If Black takes on b2, the rook to b1 opens the file, and with Black so undeveloped that's disaster for him — no calculation needed. So the plan is the knight to b3 and the rook to e1.
Black plays the knight to b4 — a good move, but it doesn't change our approach; we're in no rush to grab the d4-pawn.
The knight to b3. In this system it's fine to give up the light-squared bishop — not ideal, but survivable — and Black keeps neglecting his kingside, which could get costly.
After the capture on d3, the queen recapture loses to the bishop to b5, so we take with the c-pawn — which we'd want anyway, since it opens the c-file for a rook.
Black plays the rook to c8. I wouldn't rush to take on d4 — that pawn isn't going anywhere. Better to contest the c-file first with the rook to c1 and capture d4 at our leisure.
The rook to c1, and Black plays the knight to e7. Now it's a good moment to take on d4 — but which knight? We take with the f-knight, so the b3-knight can later jump into c5 with queenside pressure.
The f-knight takes d4, and Black recaptures with the knight to c6. I'm also thinking of dropping the bishop back to e3.

The bishop to e3. A kingside plan to consider: pushing the pawn to f4 and f5. We're x-raying the queen with a fine position and central control — and if Black takes on e5, we have a cool discovery with the knight to c6.
Black plays the queen to a6, threatening to take on c5 — we need to react.
We take on c6. The pawn to f4 was possible too, but taking is simplest — these positions always offer three or four roughly equal options.
Black develops the bishop to b4 — but by the time it's out, we'll already have the pawn to f5, and the a2-pawn simply doesn't matter for the next twenty moves.

node.idea: We have White against a strong opponent — the pawn to e4, met by e5.
The knight to f3.
Black plays the knight to c6. At these higher ratings there's a dilemma — play the recommended Four Knights Scotch, or reach for the main repertoire against a strong player.
The knight to c3 — the Four Knights Scotch, still a powerful weapon at most levels.
Black develops the knight to f6.
The pawn to d4 — heading for the Belgrade Gambit.
Black takes on d4. This is the Belgrade — I've played it in semi-competitive games and it's far more dangerous than its reputation, dismissed as unsound since the 1970s.
The knight to d5 — the Belgrade Gambit, instead of the mainline recapture. A surprise weapon to spring on a strong player.

Black plays the pawn to h6 — a reasonable move preventing the bishop to g5, one of White's main Belgrade ideas to pressure the f6-knight. The old original Belgrade doesn't come close to equalizing, but engine analysis livens it up — here I found the bishop to d3, where the classic players instead recaptured with the bishop to f4.

The bishop to d3, then a plan of repositioning to g5. If Black plays the pawn to d6, take the knight and reroute the bishop to b5 to regain d4. The bishop to c5 is possible but risky — the queenside storm with a3 and b4 can force it to lose contact with the d-pawn while opening a fianchetto square for us; and long-term, the h6 weakness invites a sacrifice on h6 once Black castles.

Black plays the pawn to d6. The key idea: the knight takes d5 is almost always in White's favour, because recapturing on d5 kicks the c6-knight and risks the d4-pawn — and if Black takes on d5 too early, a rook to e1 massacres him down the e-file. So the line goes the knight takes f6, the queen recaptures, then the bishop to b5.
The bishop to b5. If Black grabs the e4-pawn I'm not scared at all — we just castle with a huge development lead. So I like the bishop to b5 immediately.

The bishop occupies d5 as a major outpost — but the ideal piece for that square is a knight, and e2 is the transit route, via c3 or f4, to d5. Instead of h3 we can leave the bishop where it is and castle, then play f3 to chase it, unpin the knight, and build a central pawn chain — while keeping an eye on the check on f3.

If Black sacrifices the knight on f3 and recaptures with the bishop — the classic queen-to-the-g-file pattern — we have the queen to d3: it unpins the knight so it can block a check on g3, and pre-empts the exposure, keeping a lateral defence. So we castle — a bit scary, but White is clearly better. Out of the opening into the middlegame, our biggest asset is the d5-square plus fine piece coordination.
Black's weak pawns and underdeveloped kingside give us the tempi for central pressure. Black plays the bishop to e7.
The pawn to e5 looks almost winning intuitively — I'm leaning toward smashing through the barricades with tactics.

When you see a queen out early on f6, think of the piece that most commonly attacks it — the knight. So the knight to d5 leaps to mind, forcing the queen back. This is exactly why we put the bishop on e3 and not f4: on f4, Black would have the counter-strike knight to f3 with check, winning the queen.

Notice how damaging c5 was — the d5-knight is a monster. But it's moot: we have forced mate. A good example of not rushing — the queen takes h8, the king to d7, the bishop to b5 is nearly as good, but the most accurate is to start with the bishop to b5, taking away the king's escape square.

node.idea: We open the King's Gambit — a romantic opening as old as European chess itself, dating to the 16th century.
We play f4, offering the gambit pawn.
Declining with ...d6 is passive; more critically Black takes on f4, and White answers with d4.
Black holds the extra pawn with ...g5 — otherwise the gambit makes no sense — and here h4 is the main line, the bishop to c4 a rarer try.

After h4 ...g4, the flashy knight to g5 is interesting but probably unsound — the real move is the knight back to g1: you've softened f4 enough that undeveloping is justified. And against ...g4 the thematic idea is to sacrifice the knight and castle — a Muzio Gambit in spirit, sound because of White's huge lead in development and Black's exposed king.
